Indeed, what am I?— everyone does these things; they indulge in sicknesses, and I, perhaps, more than anyone else. Let's not argue; my objection is foolish. Yet, I am strongly convinced that not only a great deal of consciousness, but even any consciousness is sickness. I stand by that. Let's set that aside for a moment. Tell me this: why did it happen, as if deliberately, that in the very same minutes, the very same minutes, when I was most capable of perceiving all the nuances of "everything beautiful and sublime," as we used to say, I didn't perceive, but did such unsightly deeds, such deeds... well, let's say, that even though everyone probably does them, they seemed to happen to me precisely at those times when I was most conscious, that I shouldn't have done them at all? The more I was conscious of goodness and of all that "beautiful and sublime," the deeper I sank into my despair and the more I became completely entangled in it. But the main feature was that it seemed as if it was not by chance within me, but as if it was meant to be like that. As if this was my most normal state, and not sickness and corruption, so that, finally, I no longer had the desire to fight this corruption. It ended with me almost believing (maybe, indeed, I did believe), that this, perhaps, is my normal state. At first, in the beginning, I endured so much torment in this struggle! I didn't believe that it would happen to others, and so I kept it a secret all my life. I was ashamed (perhaps, I am still ashamed); it reached a point where I could feel a certain secret, abnormal, unworthy enjoyment returning, say, on some wretched St. Petersburg night, back to my corner, and intensely perceive that I had done another wicked thing, that there was no way to undo it, and feel it internally, secretly, bite, bite myself for it with my teeth, gnaw, gnaw and gnaw myself until the pain turned into some shameful, accursed sweetness and finally—into resolute, serious enjoyment! Yes, into enjoyment, into enjoyment! I stand by that. I spoke because I wanted, perhaps, to find out: are there such enjoyments in others? I will explain: the enjoyment was here precisely from an excessively clear perception of my humiliation; from the fact that I felt it myself to the last degree; that it was filthy, but that it couldn't be any other way; that there was no way out for me, that I would never become another person; that if there was still time and faith left to become something else, I myself would not want to become something else; I would not want to change, because in truth, I might not be able to change. And the main thing and the final point is that all this happens according to the normal and fundamental laws of intensified perception and inertia, directly flowing from these laws, so here not only can't you change, but you won't be able to do anything. In short, for example, due to an intensified perception: yes, you're a scoundrel, as if this is a scoundrel's consolation, if you already feel that you are really a scoundrel. But enough... Ah, I've explained myself, what did I explain?... What explains this enjoyment? But I will explain myself! I will bring it to an end! I took up my pen...

K. waited anxiously for a new communication each day of the following week, unable to believe that his refusal of interrogations had been taken literally, and when the expected communication had not come by Saturday evening, he assumed he had been silently summoned to the same house for the same time again. He therefore went there again on Sunday, taking the direct route via stairs and corridors; some people who remembered him greeted him at their doors, but he had to ask no one anymore and soon reached the correct door. Upon knocking, he was immediately answered, and without glancing at the familiar woman who stood by the door, he wanted to go straight into the side room. "There is no session today," the woman said. "Why shouldn't there be a session?" he asked and couldn't believe it. But the woman convinced him when she opened the door to the side room. It was truly empty and looked even more pitiable in its emptiness than the previous Sunday. On the table, which remained on the podium, lay some books. "May I look at the books?" K. asked, not out of special curiosity, but only to avoid being completely useless here. "No," the woman said and closed the door again, "that is not allowed. The books belong to the investigating judge."

"Please be concise. Time was limited for the gentlemen. It seemed unusual to me. The young people sat and stared at me with an overbearing, professional curiosity they had learned. The doctor, whom I knew, stroked his black mustache and smiled distractedly. I thought I might break into tears, but I heard myself speak in French: 'I have already had the honor, Sir, to provide you with all the information I can. Is it necessary for these gentlemen to be informed? If so, after our conversation, you will certainly be able to do so with a few words, while it is very difficult for me.' The doctor rose with a courteous smile, approached the window with his assistants and said a few words, which he accompanied with a horizontal, swaying hand movement. After three minutes, one of the young men, short-sighted and restless, returned to the table and asked, trying to stare sternly at me: 'You sleep well, Sir?' 'No, poorly.' To which he immediately jumped back to the group. They negotiated for a while, then the doctor turned to me and informed me that I would be called. I reminded him that I had been summoned by the hour. He smiled and made a few quick, jerky movements with his small white hands, which meant that he was incredibly busy. So I returned to my pacing, in which the air had become much heavier, and began to walk back and forth again, though I felt utterly exhausted. Eventually, the damp, accumulated smell made me dizzy; I stood at the entrance door and opened it slightly. I saw that it was still afternoon and a little sun outside, and that did me unspeakable good."

About the stranger who arrived, it seemed he avoided talking much; but when he did speak, he did so with generalities, with notable humility, and the conversation then took on a somewhat literary tone: that he was an insignificant worm of this world and not worthy of much concern, that he had experienced much in his lifetime, suffered in the service of truth, had many enemies who had even attempted to take his life, and that now, wishing to rest, he was seeking to find a final place to live, and that, having arrived in this city, he felt it his duty to pay his respects to the first city officials. That was all that was learned about this new face, which very soon did not hesitate to show itself at the governor's ball. The preparations for the ball took more than two hours, and in the newcomer's case, there was a level of attention to the bathroom that was not always seen. After a short afternoon nap, he ordered them to bring soap and wash his cheeks excessively long, propping them from the inside with his tongue; then, taking a napkin from the waiter's shoulder, he wiped his entire face with it, starting from the ears and twice flicking his face in the waiter's face. Then he put on a cap before the mirror, combed back the two hairs that had emerged from his nose, and immediately appeared in a burgundy-colored coat with a sparkle. Dressed in this way, he rode in his own carriage along the infinitely wide streets, illuminated by thin lighting from somewhere beyond the ocean. However, the governor's house was sufficiently lit, even for a ball; the carriage with lanterns, two soldiers stationed before the entrance, the cries of the guard at a distance - in a word, everything was as it should be. Upon entering the hall, Chichikov had to squint his eyes for a minute because the light from the candles, lamps, and women's dresses was overwhelming. Everything was bathed in light. Black coats glimmered and were scattered here and there, like flies on a shining, glittering pastry during a hot July summer, when the old housekeeper cuts and divides it into sparkling shards before an open window; the children all gather around to watch, following the movements of her stiff hands as she lifts the hammer, while the airborne squadrons of flies, lifted by a light breeze, boldly fly in as if they were the owners, taking advantage of the old woman's shortsightedness and the sun that bothered her eyes, and they scatter sweet treats wherever they land, wherever there is a crack, in thick clumps. Swollen with the summer heat, and always laying out sweet treats at every step, they didn't come to eat but to show off, to pass back and forth over the sugar pile, to rub their hind legs against each other, or to scratch themselves under their wings, or, extending both their front paws, to rub themselves against themselves above their heads, turn around, and fly away again, only to return with new persistent squadrons. Chichikov didn't even have time to look around before he was grabbed by the governor, who introduced him to the governor's wife immediately. The new guest did not drop his composure even then: he made a suitable compliment for a middle-aged man of middling rank. When the established pairs of dancers pressed everyone against the wall, he, placing his hands behind his back, looked at them for two full minutes very attentively. Many women were well-dressed and fashionable, while others were dressed as God sent to the provincial city. The men there, as everywhere, were of two kinds: those who surrounded the women and some of whom were so similar to those from St. Petersburg that it was difficult to tell them apart, had very carefully and tastefully combed-back hairstyles, or simply clean-shaven oval faces, carelessly sitting near the women, saying things in French and courting them as they did in St. Petersburg. The other kind of men were the heavyset or those who were similar in size to Chichikov, that is, not too heavy, but not thin either. These, on the contrary, bowed to the women and looked only to the sides, not arranging a green table for the cards dealer. Their faces were round and full, and some even had beard-like growths, their hair on their heads was neither worn high nor low, but parted or combed back, and their features were more rounded and strong. These were the respected officials of the city. Unfortunately, the heavyset know how to manage their affairs better in this world than the thin ones. The thin ones serve mainly on special assignments or only exist and flit here and there; their existence is too light, too airy, and completely unreliable. The heavyset never take indirect positions, but always direct ones, and if they sit somewhere, they sit firmly and solidly, so that the place may quake and crumble under them, while they will not fall. They dislike superficial shine; their coats are not tailored as skillfully as the thin ones, but they have blessings in their pockets. In three years, the thin one does not save a single soul from being put into a pawnshop; the heavyset live peacefully, just look - and here, at the end of the city, a house appears bought in the name of his wife, then another house appears on the other side of the city, then a village nearby, then a whole estate with all the land. Finally, having served God and the state, having earned universal respect, the heavyset leave service, become landowners, distinguished Russian barons, and live well. After him, the thin inheritors descend, according to Russian custom, on all the father's wealth. It cannot be hidden that such thoughts occupied Chichikov's mind while he surveyed society, and the result of this was that he finally joined the heavyset, where he met almost all the familiar faces: the prosecutor with very dark, thick eyebrows and a slightly winking left eye, as if he were saying, "Let's go, brother, to another room, there I will tell you something," - a man, however, who was serious and taciturn; the postmaster, a short man, but a keen and philosophical one; the chairman of the court, a very reasonable and kind man, - who all greeted him as an old acquaintance, to which Chichikov bowed slightly, albeit with pleasure. Here he also met the very polite and courteous landowner Manilov and the slightly clumsy in appearance Sobachichev, who accidentally kicked him with his foot and said, "I beg your pardon." Here he was given a card for cards, which he accepted with the same polite bow. They sat at the green table and did not stand up again until dinner. All conversations suddenly stopped, as they often do when people finally turn to practical matters. Although the postmaster was very talkative, the one who took the cards in his hand expressed a thoughtful expression on his face, covered his lower lip with his upper lip, and kept this position throughout the game. Upon leaving the game, he struck the table hard with his hand, ordering, if it was a woman: "Go, old grandmother!", if it was a king: "Go, Tambov peasant!" Occasionally, upon striking the cards on the table, exclamations were heard: "Ah! was not, no reason, such a bubble!", or simply exclamations: "Worms! Wormhole! Pickens!", or: "Pickens! Picking! The monkey had no trace of a mischievous monkey whatsoever, only stiff branches that had survived frost and snow. The crowd, upon seeing it, clapped and laughed heartily, calling out, "What a monkey! What a monkey!" Their uproar awakened the ancient master. The ancient master hurriedly picked up his staff and went out to ask, "Who is causing all this noise?" Upon hearing the call, the crowd hurriedly composed themselves, straightened their clothes, and bowed. Monkey appeared with his true form among the foliage and said, "Please, venerable master, my companions and I are here to give a performance. There is no one else causing this disturbance." The ancient master roared angrily, "You all shout and laugh boisterously. This is not the demeanor of a person in training. A person in training should emit a calm spiritual aura and speak with discernment. How can you make such a ruckus?!" The crowd replied, "We did not deceive you, Master. Monkey just shapeshifted to amuse the children. He transformed into a pine tree, and it truly became a pine tree. The disciples all praised and exclaimed, which caused the commotion to attract your attention, seeking forgiveness for our mistake." The ancient master said, "You all leave." He called, "Monkey, come here! I want to ask you about your actions. Why did you shape-shift and transform into a pine tree? This trickery, is it appropriate to show off in front of others? If you see someone else doing it, should you not demand that they stop? If others see you doing it, they will surely seek you out. If you fear harm, you must pass it on; if you do not pass it on, it will surely cause harm. You cannot protect your life and destiny." Monkey knocked and said, "I only beg for your forgiveness, Master." The ancient master said, "I do not blame you, but you must leave." Monkey wept upon hearing this, "Master, you told me to come from the Eastern Tang Realm's Divine Peach Blossom Mountain, Cloud-Covered River, and Celestial Waterfall Cave." The ancient master said, "You must return quickly, for your life and destiny cannot be guaranteed here." Monkey acknowledged his guilt, "I will report to the venerable master, I have been away from home for twenty years. Although I yearn to revisit my relatives and friends, I cannot go due to Master's great kindness and the unpaid debt." The ancient master said, "There is no virtue or debt where you come from. You are only to not cause trouble or involve me."

K was interrupted by a scream from the audience. He squinted his eyes to see, as the gray light of the day made the fog white and dazzling. It was the washerwoman whom K had recognized upon her entrance as a significant disturbance. Whether she was guilty or not could not be determined. K saw that a man had pulled her into a corner by the door and was holding her. However, it was not she who was screaming, but the man, who had opened his mouth wide and was looking up at the ceiling. A small circle had formed around the two, with gallery-goers nearby appearing to be thrilled that the gravity K had brought into the assembly was interrupted in this manner. K wanted to rush towards them at first impression, thinking that everyone would be interested in establishing order and at least showing the pair out of the hall, but the first rows in front of him remained completely still, no one stirred, and no one allowed K through. On the contrary, they held him back, old men putting out their arms, and some unseen hand – he did not have time to turn around – grasped him from behind by the collar. K was not really thinking about the pair any more, as if his freedom was being restricted, as if there was serious arrest being made, and he jumped down from the podium carelessly. Now he stood face to face with the crowd. Had he misjudged the people? Had he given his speech too much credence? Had they feigned indifference while he was speaking, and were now, as he came to his conclusions, feigning shock? What faces surrounded him! Small, black eyes darted here and there, the faces hung down like those of the dazed, the long beards were stiff and sparse, and when one grabbed them, it was as if one was merely clawing, not grabbing hair. But beneath the beards – and this was the discovery that K made – badges gleamed on the collar of the coats in various sizes and colors. All of them had these badges, as far as one could see. All of them belonged to each other, the apparent parties to the right and left, and as he suddenly turned around, he saw the same badges on the collar of the judge, who stood calmly with his hands in his pockets, looking down. "So," K cried out and threw his arms up, the sudden realization wanting space, "you are all officials, as I can see, you are the corrupt faction, against which I spoke, you have crowded in here as listeners and sniffers, have created false parties, and one applauded to test me, you wanted to learn how to lead the innocent astray! Now, you have not been in vain here, I hope, either you have discussed among yourselves that someone expected the defense of your innocence, or – let me or I'll hit you," K shouted at an old man who had pushed himself particularly close to him – "or else you have really learned something. And I wish you success in your profession." He quickly picked up his hat, which was on the edge of the table, and pushed his way out through the crowd, under the most complete silence, if not of surprise, then of shock. The judge seemed to have appeared even faster than K, for he was waiting for him at the door. "Just a moment," he said. K stopped, but he did not look at the judge, but at the door, whose latch he had already grabbed. "I just wanted to draw your attention to the fact," the judge said, "that you have today – it may not have occurred to you yet – deprived yourself of the advantage that a hearing for the accused always means." K laughed at the door. "You scoundrels," he cried, "I give you all hearings," he opened the door and rushed down the stairs. Behind him, the noise of the revived assembly began to rise, which was probably beginning to discuss the events in the manner of students.

Mity stepped out from behind the curtain and stood motionless. The room was filled with people, not crowded, but entirely new. A chill ran down his spine, and he jumped. He recognized all these people instantly. There was this tall, plump old man, in a coat and with a fur hat with a cockade - it was the warden, Michail Makarych. That "hunchbacked" well-groomed dandy, "always in such polished boots" - that was the prosecutor's colleague. "He has a pocket watch worth four hundred rubles, he showed it." That young, small, bespectacled man... Mity had forgotten his last name, but he knew him too - he had seen him: he was the investigator, the investigating judge, "from Legal Studies", who had recently arrived. That one over there - the militia officer, Maurits Maurititch, that one he knew well, a familiar face. What about those with badges, what were they there for? And there were two more men of some kind... And there, by the door, were Kalganov and Trifon Borisitch...

In the course of the first day, the father laid out the entire financial situation and prospects, not only for the mother but also for the sister. Here and there, he stood up from the table and retrieved some document or ledger from his small safe, which he had salvaged from the collapse of his business five years prior. One could hear him lock the complex safe and then relock it after removing the desired item. These explanations from the father were partly the first pleasant thing that Gregor had heard since his imprisonment. He had thought that the father had not a penny left from that business, at least the father had not told him anything to the contrary, and Gregor himself had not asked him about it. Gregor's concern at that time had been only to do everything he could to make the family forget the business misfortune that had plunged them all into complete hopelessness as soon as possible. And so, he had started working with great intensity at that time and had practically overnight transformed from a small commission agent into a traveler, who, of course, had completely different opportunities for earning money, and whose earnings successes were immediately converted into cash, which could be laid on the amazed and delighted family's table at home. It was a beautiful time, and such times have never been repeated, despite the fact that Gregor later earned so much money that he was able to cover the expenses of the entire family and even paid for them. People had simply gotten used to both the family and Gregor, accepting the money gratefully and willingly supplying it, but a special warmth could no longer be felt. Only the sister had remained close to Gregor, and it was his secret plan to send her, who, unlike Gregor, loved music and played the violin with feeling, to the conservatory next year, regardless of the high costs that this would entail and which would be made up for in some other way. The conservatory was often mentioned in conversations with the sister during Gregor's brief stays in the city, but always only as a beautiful dream, the realization of which was not to be considered, and the parents did not even listen to these innocent mentions with pleasure; but Gregor thought very determinedly about it and intended to announce it formally on Christmas Eve.

It required incredible caution to live with this blood. The Duke was ensnared within himself, and at times feared, when it was around him, hidden and dark. It could even be terrifyingly foreign to him, this nimble, half-Portuguese blood, which he scarcely knew. Often it frightened him, that it might attack him in his sleep and tear him apart. He acted as though he controlled it, but he always stood in his fear. He dared never to love a woman, lest it become jealous, and it was so fierce that wine never passed his lips; instead, he soothed himself with rose water. However, once, in the camp before Lausanne, when Granson was lost, he drank much pure wine. But then his blood slept. In his senseless final years, it sometimes fell into these heavy, bestial sleep. Then it revealed how much he was under its control; for when it slept, he was nothing. Then none from his surroundings were allowed to enter; he did not understand what they spoke. He could not show himself to the foreign envoys, so empty was he. Then he sat and waited, until it awoke.

Dasha and her husband could not draw much consolation from the news, especially at first. Sonya continued to report that he was always morose, taciturn, and almost entirely uninterested in the news she relayed to him from the letters she received; that he occasionally asked about his mother; and when she, seeing that he was already anticipating the truth, finally told him about her death, to her surprise, even the news of his mother's death did not seem to affect him much, at least that was her impression from the outside. Sonya reported, among other things, that despite appearing to be completely immersed in himself and cut off from everyone else, he approached his new life very directly and simply, that he was clearly aware of his situation, did not expect anything better nearby, had no frivolous hopes (which was characteristic of his situation), and was almost unaffected by the new surroundings around him, which were so unlike anything before. Sonya reported that his health was satisfactory. He goes to work, refusing neither to avoid nor accept it. He is almost indifferent to food, but that the food, except on Sundays and holidays, was so bad that, in the end, he accepted some money from Sonya to start having tea every day; as for the rest, he asked her not to worry, assuring her that all these concerns only annoyed him. Sonya also reported that his living conditions in the fortress were shared with everyone else, she had not seen the inside of their barracks, but concluded that it was cramped, shabby, and unhealthy; that he slept on a straw mat, laying a woolen blanket beneath himself, and did not want to make any other arrangements for himself. However, he lived so crudely and frugally not according to any prejudiced plan or intention, but simply due to negligence and external indifference to his fate. Sonya wrote directly that he, especially at first, not only showed no interest in her visits, but even almost resented her, was taciturn and even gruff with her, but that in the end these visits had become a habit and almost a necessity for him, so that he was very anxious when she was ill for a few days and could not visit him. It seems that she sees him at the gates of the fort on holidays or in the guardhouse, where he is called to her for several minutes; on weekdays, however, when she visits him at work, in the workshops, at brick factories, or at sheds on the banks of the Irtysh. Sonya informed herself that she had been able to make some acquaintances and connections in the city; that she was sewing, and since there were almost no dressmakers in the city, she became necessary in many households; she did not mention that through her and Raskolnikov received the patronage of the authorities, that his work was made easier and so on. Finally, news came (Dasha even noticed some unusual anxiety and worry in her last letters) that he shuns everyone, that the convicts in the fortress did not take a liking to him; that he was silent for whole days and became very pale. Suddenly, in the last letter, Sonya wrote that he was very seriously ill and lying in the hospital, in the prison ward...

P.S. "kordegar'diya" refers to the guards at a gate or checkpoint. It is a term used in the Russian Empire to describe the military detachment stationed at various gates, bridges, or other strategic points to control the movement of people and goods. In this context, it appears to be a place where Sonya and Dasha's husband meet or communicate.

For the third time, Ivan Fedorovich had gone to speak with Smerdyakov upon his return from Moscow. The first time after the tragedy, he saw him and spoke with him on the very first day of his arrival, then visited him again two weeks later. However, after that second meeting with Smerdyakov, Ivan Fedorovich ceased those meetings, so it's been over a month since he last saw him and hardly heard anything about him. Upon his return from Moscow, Ivan Fedorovich had only been gone for five days following his parent's death, so he did not even catch the burial: the funeral had taken place the day before his arrival. The delay in Ivan Fedorovich's return was due to Alyosha, unaware of his exact Moscow address, resorting to Katya for sending a telegram. In turn, Katya, also unaware of the true address, telegraphed to her sister and aunt, hoping that Ivan Fedorovich would visit them as soon as he arrived in Moscow. However, he did not visit them until the fourth day after his arrival, and upon reading the telegram, he immediately flew to us. Upon first meeting, Alyosha was greeted by us, but after talking to him, we were surprised to find that he did not even suspect Mitya, but rather directly pointed the finger at Smerdyakov as the murderer, which was in direct contrast to all other opinions in our town. After seeing the inspector and the prosecutor, learning the details of the accusation and arrest, we were even more surprised by Alyosha and attributed his opinion to his extremely agitated brotherly feelings and compassion for Mitya, whom Alyosha, as Ivan knew, deeply loved. Incidentally, let me just say a few words about Ivan's feelings for his brother Dmitry Fyodorovich: he decisively did not love him and often felt compassion for him, mixed with a great amount of contempt, bordering on spite. Mitya, in every way, was extremely unappealing to him. Ivan looked at Katya's love for Mitya with indignation. Nevertheless, he also saw Mitya on his first day in Moscow, and this meeting did not weaken his belief in his guilt, but rather strengthened it. He found Mitya in distress, in a painful state of agitation. Mitya spoke at length, but was scattered and disorganized, speaking very sharply, accusing Smerdyakov and getting tangled up terribly. He spoke most of all about the same three thousand rubles, which "stole" from him the deceased. "My money, they were my money," Mitya asserted, "if I had even stolen them, I would have been right." Almost all the evidence against him he did not contest and, if he interpreted the facts in his favor, he did so very awkwardly and ineptly - in general, as if he did not even want to justify himself before Ivan or anyone, on the contrary, he grew angry, arrogantly ignored the accusations, defended himself and fumed. He treated Gregory's testimony about the open door with contempt, laughing scornfully and insisting that it was "the devil who opened it." However, he could not present any coherent explanations for this fact. He even managed to offend Ivan Fedorovich in this first meeting, sharply telling him that he should not suspect and interrogate him, who himself claimed that "everything is allowed." In general, he was very unfriendly towards Ivan Fedorovich on this occasion. After this meeting with Mitya, Ivan Fedorovich then proceeded to Smerdyakov.

The delay in Ivan Fedorovich's visit was due to Aleksey, who did not know his exact Moscow address, using Katerina Ivanovna to send a telegram. Katerina Ivanovna, also in the dark about his actual address, telegraphed to her sister and aunt, expecting Ivan Fedorovich to visit them immediately upon his arrival in Moscow. But he did not visit them until the fourth day of his arrival, and, after reading the telegram, immediately left for us. Upon his first meeting, Alyosha was greeted by him, but, after speaking with him, was very surprised that he did not even suspect Mitya, but pointed directly to Smerdyakov as the murderer, which was contrary to all other opinions in our town. After meeting the inspector and the prosecutor, learning the details of the accusation and the arrest, he was even more surprised by Alyosha and attributed his opinion to nothing more than intense fraternal feeling and compassion for Mitya, whom Alyosha, as Ivan knew, loved very much. It should be mentioned in passing that Ivan's feelings for his brother Dmitry Fedorovich were unrequited, and he often felt sympathy for him, mixed with a great contempt bordering on contempt. Mitya, even his entire physical form, was extremely unattractive to him. Ivan looked on Katerina Ivanovna's love for Mitya with disgust. However, on the first day of his arrival, he also saw Mitya, and this meeting did not weaken his belief in his guilt, but rather strengthened it. He found Mitya in distress, in painful agitation. Mitya was talkative, but scattered and disorganized, spoke very sharply, accused Smerdyakov and became terribly confused. Above all, he spoke extensively about the same three thousand rubles, which he had "stolen" from him. "My money, they were mine," Mitya said, "If I had even stolen them, I would have been right." Almost all the evidence against him, he did not deny, and, if he explained the facts in his favor, he did so very sloppily and foolishly – in general as if he did not want to justify himself at all before Ivan or anyone else, on the contrary, became angry, proudly disregarded the accusations, defended himself and raged. He laughed scornfully at the testimony of Grigory about the open door, and assured that it was "the devil who opened it." But he could not provide any coherent explanations for this fact. He even managed to offend Ivan Fedorovich in this first meeting, sharply telling him that he was not the one to suspect and interrogate, who themselves claim that "everything is allowed." In general, on this occasion, he was very unfriendly to Ivan Fedorovich. After this meeting with Mitya, Ivan Fedorovich went to Smerdyakov.

There was virtually nothing to do. I walked around the city and noted that it had changed. It was pleasant for me to step out of the hotel I had checked into, and to see that it was now a city for adults, coming together almost as if for a stranger. Everything had become a bit smaller, and I strolled along Langelinie out to the lighthouse and back. When I arrived in the area of Amaliengade, it was certainly possible that something might come out of somewhere that had been recognized for years and was still trying to exert its power. There were certain window corners or arches or lamps that seemed to know a lot and thus threatened. I looked them straight in the face and let them feel that I was staying at the Phoenix Hotel and could leave at any moment. But my conscience was not at ease. The suspicion arose in me that none of these influences and connections had really been dealt with. They had been abandoned one day, incomplete as they were. Childhood, too, would therefore be something to make up for, if one did not want to lose it forever. And as I realized that I was losing it, I felt at the same time that I would never have anything else, that I was being called upon to do so.

In the midst of the commotion, Yuanjun arrived and asked, "Brothers, have you not seen him in that chamber?" The gods replied, "He was just surrounded, and thus became invisible." Sanzang round-eyed like a phoenix, witnessing the Great Sage transform into a sparrow and affix it to a tree, took away the law image, discarded the divine weapon, shook off his armor, transformed into a hawk-eagle, flapped his wings, and prepared to strike. The Great Sage saw this and spread one wing, transforming into an enormous seagull, ascending towards the heavens. Sanzang saw this and flapped his feathers, transforming into a great crane, climbing the celestial path to meet. The Great Sage again made himself solid, entering a ravine, transforming into a fish and submerging into the water. Sanzang rushed to the edge of the ravine but found no trace. In his heart, he thought, "This monkey must have also dived into the water. It will certainly transform into fish or shrimp types. I will change and capture it again." Indeed, he transformed into a fish-hawk, drifting on the water's surface. After a moment, the Great Sage transformed into a fish, swimming with the current, suddenly seeing a flying creature resembling a green parrot, with feathers that were not green; resembling a duck or a swan, with no crest; resembling an old crane, with legs that were not red: "It seems to be Sanzang transforming to wait for me." He turned around, fleeing after making a flower bloom. Sanzang saw this and thought, "The blooming fish is like a carp, without red fins; like a turtle, without scales; like a black fish, without stars on its head; like a catfish, without spines on its cheeks. How could it have seen me and returned? It must be the monkey that has transformed." He hurried over and nipped at one bite. The Great Sage, recognizing this, emerged from the water, transforming into a water snake, swimming close to the shore and burrowing into the grass. Sanzang, unable to catch him, saw the water splashing and saw a snake emerge, recognizing it as the Great Sage, he quickly transformed into a jujube-capped gray crane, with a long beak resembling an iron spike, rushing to catch the water snake. The water snake jumped about, transforming into a flower bird, standing motionless on the marshy bank. Sanzang, seeing it become lowly,—flower birds being the most filthy and lewd of birds, not discriminating between hawks, phoenixes, eagles, or crows—thus did not approach to embrace, immediately reverted to his original form, walking away, drawing his bow and filling it, releasing one arrow to strike the flower bird, hitting it on the foot.

In the commotion, the True King arrived, asking, "Brothers, have you not seen him in that room?" The gods replied, "He was surrounded here and disappeared. He was enveloped and thus could not be seen." Sanzang blinked his phoenix eyes to watch as the Great Sage transformed into a sparrow, nailed to a tree. He took back his sacred emblem, discarded his divine weapon, shed his human form, and transformed into a bird of prey, spreading his wings and taking flight to attack. Upon seeing this, the Great Sage spread his wings and transformed into a large sea hawk, soaring into the sky. Sanzang, upon seeing this, ruffled his feathers, transformed into a large crane, ascended to the heavens, and pursued. The Great Sage dove, reverted back to his original form, and transformed into a fish, swimming in the water. Sanzang reached the edge of the stream but did not see any traces. He suspected in his heart, "This fox-spirit must have gone into the water. It will surely transform into a fish or shrimp. I will wait and transform again to catch it." He transformed into a fish-eagle, floating on the water's surface. After a short while, the Great Sage transformed into a fish, swimming with the current. Suddenly, a flying bird appeared, resembling a green parrot, its feathers not green; resembling a duck, it had no crest; resembling an eagle, it had no red legs: "I think this must be Sanzang, disguising himself to lure me." He swiftly turned away and flew off. Sanzang observed, "That flying fish, it resembles a carp, its tail is not red; it resembles a snakehead, its scales are not visible; it resembles a black carp, it has no stars on its head; it resembles a sturgeon, it has no spines on its cheeks. Why did it leave after seeing me? It must have been that monkey who transformed. I'll catch up." He approached and took a bite. The Great Sage, recognizing him, emerged from the water, transformed into a water snake, swam close to the shore, and hid in the grass. Sanzang was unable to grab him, so he saw the water splash and the appearance of a snake emerging. He recognized it as the Great Sage and immediately transformed into a bird with a brocade cap, a long beak resembling an iron toothed wrench, rushing to catch this water snake. The water snake jumped and transformed into a water duck, sitting motionless on the reeds. Sanzang, upon seeing it become so lowly, did not approach to greet it, but returned to his original form and walked away, taking his bow and arrows with him. He shot an arrow, hitting the water duck, killing it.

Incredibly, I managed to leave the house alone in the evening; I ran, I turned a corner, and in the same instant, I collided with him. I don't understand how this, which just happened, could unfold in about five seconds. No matter how much one tells it, it takes much longer. I had hurt myself in the rush towards him; I was small, it seemed to me already a lot that I did not cry, also I unconsciously expected to be comforted. Since he did not do that, I took him for shy; it seemed to me, I guessed, that the right joke, in which this matter could be resolved, did not occur to him. I was already happy enough to help him, but for that, it was necessary to see his face. I said that he was tall. Now he had not, as it should have been naturally, bowed over me, so that he was at a height I was not prepared for. Still, there was nothing before me but the smell and the peculiar hardness of his coat, which I felt. Suddenly his face appeared. What it was? I don't know, I don't want to know. It was the face of an enemy. And next to this face, close by, at the height of the terrible eyes, stood, like a second head, his fist. Before I had time to lower my face, I had already run; I ducked to the left past him and ran straight down an empty, frightening alley, the alley of a foreign city, a city where nothing is forgiven.

K said, emerging from contemplation, "I don't want a speaker's success," but that might be unattainable. The presiding judge likely speaks much better, as it is part of his profession. What I want is only the public discussion of a public wrong. Listen: I was arrested about ten days ago, laughing about the arrest itself, but that's not relevant here. I was surprised early in the morning, perhaps someone – as the presiding judge said, it wasn't excluded – gave the order to arrest any room painter, who is just as innocent as I am, but they chose me. The adjacent room was occupied by two rough guards. If I were a dangerous robber, they could not have taken better precautions. These guards were demoralized personnel, they chattered my ears off, they tried to bribe me, they tried to extort laundry and clothing from me, they tried to get money, to supposedly bring me breakfast after they had eaten my own breakfast shamelessly in front of me. Not enough there. I was led to a third room by the supervisor. It was the room of a woman I highly respect, and I had to watch as this room, through the presence of the guards and the supervisor, in a sense was sullied. It was not easy to remain calm. But I managed, and I asked the supervisor calmly – if he were here, he would confirm it – why I was arrested. What did this supervisor, whom I still see sitting on the chair of the said woman as a representation of the most stubborn arrogance, answer? My lords, he answered in essence nothing, perhaps he really knew nothing, he had arrested me and was satisfied with that. He had even done something extra and brought three low-level bank employees into the woman's room, who were busy handling and disorganizing her photographs, which belonged to her. The presence of these employees had of course another purpose; they were to, just like my landlady and her maid, spread the news of my arrest, damage my public image, and in particular in the bank to shake my position. Now, nothing of that has succeeded, not in the least, even my landlady, a simple person – I will name her here with respect, her name is Frau Grubach – even Frau Grubach was smart enough to see that such an arrest does not mean more than a prank, which unsupervised boys on the street could carry out. I repeat, the whole thing has only caused me inconvenience and temporary annoyance, but it could also have more serious consequences?

Only because the Queen Mother ate peaches, she held a feast at the Jade Pool and invited all guests. At that time, everyone was drunk and the atmosphere was chaotic, with people stumbling and splashing about. The hero barged into the palace of Broad Han. Graceful fairies came to greet him. Seeing his appearance, which was able to captivate the souls of men, they found it difficult to forget the old days. He had no sense of hierarchy, pulling the moon goddess to stay with him. Again and again, he refused to comply, hiding in the east and evading in the west, showing displeasure. His courage was like thunder, almost causing the gates of heaven to tremble. He reported to the Jade Emperor about this matter, and the Jade Emperor announced that he would make the decision on that day. Broad Han surrounded him, making it difficult for him to escape. However, various gods took hold of him. Despite the wine in his mind, he did not yield. He was led to the palace of the spirits in the sky to be questioned by the Jade Emperor. According to the rules, he was to be sentenced to death. Fortunately, Tai Bai Li Jinzheng spoke on his behalf, reducing his punishment to two thousand strikes. His flesh was flayed, and his bones were broken. He was expelled from heaven and banished to Fuchi Mountain, where he began his farming life. He was born with a sin, and his nickname is Pig Iron. "The Traveler heard the words and said: 'This fellow is actually a god of the Tianbo Water, a being from the underworld. He recognizes my family name.' The monster said with a sigh: 'You, this false Pantaloon, when you caused disaster that time, you didn't know how much you affected us. Today, you come to deceive us again!' Don't be disrespectful, try my club!'" The traveler did not tolerate the situation and picked up a stick, hitting him directly on the head. The two of them fought on a half-mountain under the dark night. The traveler's eyes shone like electricity, and the monster's eyes shone like silver flowers. The monster sprayed colored smoke, and the traveler breathed out red mist. The red mist made the darkness clear, and the colored smoke made the night bright. The iron club and the nine-toothed club, both heroes were worth praising: one was the Holy One coming to the mortal world, and the other was the Marshal descending to the earth's end. The one who became a monster due to losing his dignity, and the other who escaped from hardship to become a monk. The nine-toothed club went as if a dragon was stretching its claws, and the iron club welcomed like a phoenix passing through flowers. The monster accused him of killing his own family and the other accused him of raping a young girl. They talked idly, argued recklessly, and often fought with clubs and knives. Looking at their fight until the break of dawn, the monster felt pain in his arms. They fought from the second watch until the east was bright. The monster was unable to withstand the enemy, retreated and returned to his hole, closing the door tightly, not appearing again. The traveler saw a stone monument outside the hole with the words "Cloud Stack Cave" inscribed on it. Seeing the monster did not come out, the sky became clear, but his heart still thought: "I wonder if my master is waiting, I will go back to see him, and I will come back to capture this monster without delay." He walked lightly, quickly returning to the High Old Manor.

(Note: Pantaloon is a character from Italian comic opera, who is often depicted wearing tight pants that are loose at the knees and are held up by a band around his waist. This term was used in a sarcastic or disrespectful way in this context.)

The east was leaning to the west, and chaos reigned. A man of valor barged into the Grand Cold Palace, and a graceful immortal came to greet him. Upon seeing his appearance, which was difficult to extinguish, the hearts of the old days could not be eradicated. He was neither arrogant nor humble, and he attempted to make Jade-Hair pull her along. Again and again, he refused to comply, and the east hid in the west, and his heart was not in agreement. His spirit was like the thunder, and he almost frightened the celestial city. He inquired about the spiritual officials and reported to the Jade Emperor. At that time, I would have to make a decision about his fate. The Grand Cold Palace was surrounded and could not be breached, and there was no way in or out. Yet, the various gods caught hold of me, and the wine was still not cowardly in my heart. I was led to the Spiritual Sky to see the Jade Emperor, and I was questioned according to the rules. And he looked at the alarm clock on the bedside table, which was ticking. "Heavenly Father!" he thought, It was half seven o'clock, and the hands were moving calmly forward, it was almost over, it was nearing quarter to. Had the alarm not rung? One could see from the bed that it was correctly set for four o'clock; surely it had rung. Yes, but was it possible to peacefully sleep through this furniture-shaking racket? Now, he hadn't slept peacefully, but perhaps all the more firmly. What should he do now? The next train was at seven o'clock; to catch it, he would have had to rush madly, and the collection wasn't yet packed, and he himself didn't feel particularly fresh and agile. And even if he caught the train, a storm from the boss was not to be avoided, for the office assistant had waited for the five o'clock train and the report of his absence had been made long ago. It was a creature of the boss, without backbone or sense. What now, if he called in sick? That would be extremely embarrassing and suspicious, for Gregor had been in his five-year employment yet never sick. Fear was the beginning, fear and lust and an unsettling curiosity about what was to come. Night reigned, and his senses listened; for the clamor was drawing nearer, the noise, a mix of racket: rattling, rustling, and low thunder, accompanied by shrill cheering and a particular howling in a drawn-out u-sound, all pervaded and eerily sweetened by deep, persistent flute playing that enchanted his innards. But he knew one word, dark yet defining what was approaching: "The strange god!" A slimy glow seeped: he recognized mountainous terrain, similar to that surrounding his summer home. And in torn light, from wooded heights, between tree trunks and moss-covered rocky debris, it flowed and plunged downwards in a whirl: humans, animals, a swarm, a rampaging horde, and it overwhelmed the mound with bodies, flames, tumult, and erratic dance. Women, shivering over long fur garments that hung from their waists, shook tinkling drums over their shrinking heads, swung branded torches and bare daggers, held coiled snakes in the center of their bodies, or carried screaming breasts in both hands. Men, with antlers on their foreheads, wearing fur coats and shaggy from skin, bent their necks and raised arms and thighs, let bronze cauldrons rumble and beat wildly on drums, while smooth boys with adorned staffs goaded the goats, clinging to their horns and allowing themselves to be swung around and slide in joy. And the ecstatic ones howled the call out in soft vowels and drawn-out u-sounds, wild and sweet, never heard before: here it echoed, touched by the air, like deer, and there it was repeated, in wild triumph, inciting each other to dance and flinging of limbs, never letting it cease. But the deep, luring flute tone dominated and ruled. Did it not also lure him, the reluctant witness, shamelessly persistent to the feast and excess of the ultimate sacrifice? Great was his disgust, great his fear, honest his will, until the end to protect his own against the stranger, the enemy of the contained and worthy spirit. But the noise, the howling, amplified by echoing mountain walls, grew, took control, swelled into irresistible madness. Mists pressed on the mind, the tantalizing smell of the goats, the reek of heated bodies, and a scent like of putrid water, added to it another, familiar: of wounds and surrounding sickness. With the drumbeats, his heart throbbed, his brain whirled, anger took hold of him, delusion, numbing pleasure, and his soul yearned to join the dance of the god. The obscene symbol, huge, made of wood, was unveiled and raised high: they shouted the slogan without restraint. Foaming at the mouth, they raged, teased each other with lewd gestures and fighting hands, laughed and cried,—stabbed each other with thorny staffs and licked the blood from their limbs. But with them, in them, the dreamer was now and the strange god was his. Yes, they were he, as they violently and killing threw themselves on the animals and swallowed steaming chunks, as limitless confusion began on mossy ground, in offering to the god. And his soul tasted lust and madness of the apocalypse.

Again, a sound of "Zi" was heard, and the two doors opened. The traveler meowed and flew in, only to see the old witch giving orders to the guards at each door: "I fear that the wind of yesterday did not kill Sun Wukong, he will definitely come back today, and when he comes, I will surely teach him a lesson he won't forget." The traveler heard this and flew over the hall, heading to the back. However, he saw a closed set of doors, tightly shut. The traveler peered through the cracks and tried to squeeze in, only to find it was a large courtyard. The walled room had wind chimes hanging up, binding Sun Wukong. Tang Sanzang wept, constantly thinking of Monkey and Pigsy. The traveler spread his wings, rapped on his bald head, and called out, "Master!" The old man recognized his voice and said, "Monkey, you too want to kill me? You call me here?" The traveler replied, "Master, I am on your head. Do not worry, do not be anxious, we must capture the witch, only then can we save your life." Tang Sanzang asked, "Disciple, when will we capture the witch?" The traveler replied, "The tiger demon that you had is already dead, killed by Eight Immortals. Only the witch's influence remains. I expect that she will only be here today, and I will seize her. Do not cry, I will mute her."

Upon arrival at the hut, everything was still, and from the herd came two beautiful, slender goats, one white and one brown, towards the grandfather and licked his hands, for he had a little salt in them, as he did every evening to welcome his two little animals. Peter disappeared with his flock. Heidi stroked tenderly one and then the other of the goats and skipped around them, wanting to stroke them from the other side as well, and was completely happy and joyful about the little creatures. "Are they ours, Grandfather? Are they both ours? Will they come into the stable? Will they always stay with us?", Heidi asked one after another in her pleasure, and her grandfather could barely insert his steady "Yes, yes!" between one and the other question. As the goats had licked up their salt, the Old One said, "Go and bring out your little dish and the bread."

On the contrary, Aleksei was at that time robust, ruddy-cheeked, with bright eyes, a healthy nineteen-year-old adolescent. He was at that time extremely handsome, well-built, of medium height, dark-haired, with a correct, although slightly elongated oval face, with shining dark-gray widely spaced eyes, very contemplative and apparently very calm. People might say, perhaps, that red cheeks do not hinder fanaticism or mysticism; but I think that Aleksei was even more than anyone, a realist. Oh, of course, in the monastery he completely believed in miracles, but, in my opinion, miracles do not confuse a realist. The true realist, if he is not a believer, will always find within himself the strength and ability not to believe in a miracle, and if a miracle becomes an irresistible fact before him, then he will rather not believe his feelings, than admit the fact. If he does admit it, then he will admit it as a natural fact, but until now, one that has been unknown to him. Faith in a realist is not born from a miracle, but a miracle is born from faith. If a realist believes once, then he must inevitably, because of his realism, also admit and a miracle. Thomas the Apostle declared that he would not believe until he saw, and when he saw, he said: “My Lord and my God!” Was the miracle what made him believe? It is more likely that no, and he believed only for one reason: that he wanted to believe, and perhaps he already believed fully, in the depths of his being, even then, when he said: “I will not believe until I see.”

Once, as darkness approached over this story, I was on the verge of telling Maman about the 'Hand': in that moment, I could have done it. I was about to take a breath to begin, but it occurred to me how well I understood the servant, that he could not have come to their faces. And I was afraid of Maman's face, if she were to see what I had seen. I took a quick breath again, to give the impression that I wanted nothing else. A few years later, after the peculiar night in the gallery at Urnekloster, I spent days trying to confide in little Erik. But he had completely shut himself off from me after our nightly conversation, avoiding me; I believe he despised me. And precisely because of that, I wanted to tell him about the 'Hand.' I imagined that I would win his approval (and I desperately wanted this for some reason) if I could make him understand that I had really experienced it. But Erik was so skilled at dodging that it never came to pass. And then we traveled away shortly after. Strangely enough, it was the first time I (and eventually only myself) told an event that now lies far in my childhood.

Suddenly one day, the Ancestor and the crowd of disciples were playing and performing in front of the Three Stars Cave at dusk. The Ancestor asked Tripitaka, "Have you managed to reach the level you thought you would?" Tripitaka replied, "I have received Master's boundless grace, and my disciples' accomplishments are complete. I can now perform the miracle of flying and rising into the clouds." The Ancestor said, "Show me. Try flying." Tripitaka demonstrated his ability, leaped from the ground about five to six zhang, stepped on the clouds and went, but after a brief flight, he returned without going more than three li. He landed in front of the Ancestor, crossed his hands, and said, "Master, this is flying and leaping into the clouds." The Ancestor laughed and said, "This is not really flying, only climbing clouds. It has been said from ancient times, 'The immortals travel across the northern sea and rest in the wild pines.' You, in a mere half day, have not been able to go more than three li. Even climbing clouds is not considered enough!" Tripitaka said, "How can I reach 'traveling across the northern sea and resting in the wild pines?'" The Ancestor said, "Those who truly fly will rise early from the northern sea, travel across the eastern sea, the western sea, the southern sea, and then return to the wild pines. The wild pines are actually a term for the northern sea's peak. Only by traversing the areas outside the four seas in one day can one be said to truly fly." Tripitaka said, "This is too difficult! Too difficult!" The Ancestor said, "There is no impossible task in the world, only those without determination." Upon hearing this, Tripitaka bowed his head in respect and said, "Master, 'A person should strive to be thorough,' so I willingly set aside great compassion and accept this flying technique from you. I will never forget your kindness." The Ancestor said, "Those who truly fly will stumble and then rise. You are different. I only grant you the technique of the 'String of Clouds.' " Tripitaka bowed again and asked for the technique, but the Ancestor gave him a set of instructions: "This cloud, if you twist it and recite the true words, clench your fist, shake your body, and leap, you will fly for ten million eight thousand li." Hearing this, the crowd laughed, saying, "Tripitaka is crafty! If he learns this technique, he can compete with others in sending letters, delivering messages, and delivering documents, and find food anywhere!" Master and disciple returned to their dwelling places under the sky that night. That very night, Tripitaka immediately practiced the divine cultivation technique, learned the String of Clouds, and lived freely without restraint for the rest of his long life.

One day, the master and the disciples played around sunset at the Three Stars Cave. The master asked Tripitaka, "Have you achieved what you set out to do?" Tripitaka replied, "I have received the grace of Master Sea and fulfilled my duties as a disciple. I am now able to rise and fly up to the clouds." The master said, "Try flying up and let me see." Tripitaka demonstrated his skill, stood on his tiptoes, ran and jumped off the ground about five to six feet, stepped on the clouds and grabbed a meal, returned but could not land more than three li near or far, and landed on the ground. He crossed his hands and said, "Master, this is flying up to the clouds." The master smiled and said, "This is not considered flying up to the clouds, only climbing the clouds. The ancient saying goes, 'Immortals wander north seas in the morning and rest in the South of the Misty Forest in the evening.' You, in half a day, could not travel more than three li. Even climbing the clouds, it is still not enough!" Tripitaka said, "How can I achieve 'wandering north seas in the morning and resting in the South of the Misty Forest in the evening'?" The master said, "Those who fly up to the clouds will get up early in the morning and leave the North Sea, travel across the East Sea, West Sea, and South Sea, and return to the South of the Misty Forest. The Misty Forest is just a phrase used by the North Sea. Only when you traverse all the areas outside the four seas in a day can you be considered as flying up to the clouds." Tripitaka said, "This is too difficult! This is too difficult!" The master said, "There is no impossible task in the world, only those with no heart." Hearing these words, Tripitaka bowed and asked, "Master, 'to benefit the people is to fully understand them,' please bestow upon me this method of flying up to the clouds, I will never forget your kindness." The master said, "All immortals who fly up to the clouds stumble and get up again. You, however, have only just started. I will teach you a 'Monkey Cloud'." Tripitaka bowed and pleaded again, but the master taught him a set of incantations. "This cloud, when you twist it, recite the true words, clench your fist, shake your body, and jump, you will rise into the air. A 'Monkey Cloud' has a journey of ten million eight thousand li." The crowd heard this and everyone laughed, "Monkey, you have invented a method! If you know this method, you can wage war with others, deliver messages, and deliver documents, no matter where you go, you will find food to eat!" The master and disciple retired to their caves that night. That very night, Tripitaka practiced the divine incantation and learned the Monkey Cloud. From then on, he was unconstrained and unbound, wandering freely, enjoying this long life's beauty.

Suddenly one day, the ancestor and the crowd of disciples were playing and performing at the Three Stars Cave. The ancestor asked Tripitaka, "Have your tasks been accomplished, Monkey?" Tripitaka replied, "Master, I have received Master's grace and kindness, and my disciple's accomplishments are complete. I am now capable of somersaulting in the sky." The ancestor said, "Show me." Tripitaka demonstrated, lifting his body, executing a somersault and leaping from the ground about five to six zhang (Chinese units of measurement), stepping on clouds and mist to proceed, but could not return even after circling near and far, landing in front of the ancestor. He crossed his hands and said, "Master, this is somersaulting in the clouds." The ancestor laughed and said, "This does not count as somersaulting in the clouds; it only counts as climbing the clouds. Since ancient times it is said, 'Immortals traverse the northern sea and return to the autumn grasses.' Just as you could not traverse more than three li today, even climbing the clouds is still not sufficient." Tripitaka said, "How can I achieve 'traversing the northern sea and returning to the autumn grasses?'" The ancestor said, "Those who can somersault in the clouds get up early and leave from the northern sea, travel through the eastern sea, western sea, southern sea, and return to the autumn grasses. The autumn grasses are also the slang of the northern sea's peaks. Only after traversing the seas outside the four oceans can one be said to be somersaulting in the clouds." Tripitaka said, "This is too difficult! It is too difficult!" The ancestor said, "There is no impossible task in the world, only if there is a determined person." Tripitaka heard these words, bowed his head respectfully, and asked for instruction: "Master, 'to be a man is to be thorough,' so I shall set aside my great compassion and completely receive this cloud-somersaulting technique. I will never forget this kindness." The ancestor said, "All immortals who can somersault in the clouds stumble and then rise again. You are not like this. I have only just seen you do it, and you have already taken off. I will only pass on to you the 'string-pulling cloud.' " Tripitaka again bowed his head and begged, and the ancestor passed on another incantation: "This cloud, hold the incantation tightly, move your body, recite the true words, clench your fist, shake your body, and jump up. With one string-pulling cloud, you will have a path of ten million eight thousand li." The crowd listened and laughed one by one, "Monkey, if you master this technique, you can fight with other people, deliver letters, and deliver messages, wherever you go you can find food to eat!" The master and disciple returned to their cave dwellings that night. That very night, Tripitaka immediately began practicing the cloud-pulling technique and mastered it. From then on, he lived freely without restraints, roaming leisurely for a long life.

All my verses have come about differently, so they are none.--And when I wrote my drama, how was I led astray. Was I a follower and a fool, that I needed a third party to tell the story of two people who made each other's lives hard? How easily I fell into the trap. And I should have known that this third party, who goes through all lives and literatures, this phantom of a third, who never existed, has no meaning. One must deny him. He belongs to the excuses of nature, which is always trying to divert the attention of people from its deepest secrets. He is the veil, behind which a drama plays out. He is the noise at the entrance to the silent conflict of two real people. One might think it would have been too difficult to talk about the two involved; the third, precisely because he is so unreal, is the easy part, he could be handled by all. As soon as they start their dramas, one notices the impatience to come to the third, they can hardly wait for him. As soon as he is there, everything is fine. But how boring, if he is late; nothing can happen without him, everything stands still, waits. Yes, and what if it were to remain in this stasis? What, dramatist, and you, audience who knows life, what if he were to disappear, this popular man or this presumptuous young man who fits into every marriage like a spare key? What, if for example, the devil were to take him away? Let's imagine.

Mother, Mother, whispered Gregor as he looked up at her. The Procurist had momentarily forgotten all about him; however, he could not refuse the sight of the flowing coffee multiple times, snapping his jaws aimlessly. Meanwhile, the mother was now yelling anew, fleeing from the table, and flinging herself into her husband's arms. But Gregor had no time for his parents; the Procurist was already on the stairs; his chin on the banister, Gregor saw one last time. Gregor made a dash to catch up with him as best he could; the Procurist must have sensed it, for he jumped over several steps and disappeared; "Humph!" he shouted, a sound echoing through the entire staircase. Unfortunately, this flight of the Procurist seemed to confuse the father, who until then had remained relatively composed. Instead of chasing after the Procurist himself or at least not hindering Gregor in the pursuit, he grabbed the Procurist's cane, which the latter had left with his hat and overcoat on a chair, picked up a large newspaper from the table, and began, with footstomps, to force Gregor back into his room using the cane and the newspaper. No pleading from Gregor helped, no pleas were even understood; he could only lower his head humbly, but the father continued to stomp his feet more forcefully. Meanwhile, the mother, despite the cold weather, had opened a window, and she leaned out, pressing her face far outside the window in her hands. Between the alley and the staircase, a strong draft was created, causing the window curtains to flutter and the newspapers on the table to rustle. The father's stomping and grunts grew increasingly unbearable. Gregor had little practice in walking backward, and it was going very slowly. If only he could have turned around, he would have been in his room instantly, but he feared the father's impatience, and every moment threatened him with a fatal blow from the cane in the father's hand. Eventually, Gregor had no choice but to turn back, for he realized with horror that he did not even understand the direction in reversing. He began, with constant anxious glances at the father, to turn as quickly as possible, but in reality, very slowly. Perhaps the father sensed his good intentions, for he did not interfere, but guided the turning motion from a distance with the tip of his cane. If only the father's grunts had not been so intolerable! Gregor lost all sense of direction. He was almost completely turned around when he realized, listening for the grunts, that he had even made a mistake and turned a little more in the wrong direction. When he was finally fortunate to have his head before the door opening, it turned out that his body was too wide to pass through without difficulty. The father, in his current state, of course, did not even consider opening the other door handle to create a wide enough passage for Gregor. His sole fixed idea was that Gregor should get back to his room as quickly as possible. Never would he have permitted the elaborate preparations Gregor needed to get up and possibly pass through the door. Perhaps, thinking there was no obstacle, the father was now pushing Gregor forward with great noise; it was no longer the voice of a single father, but a sound that filled the room. Gregor pushed himself – whatever would happen – into the door. One side of his body lifted, he was skewed in the door opening, his one side was badly scraped, there were ugly stains on the white door, soon he was stuck and could not move anymore, his legs dangled on one side, trembling in the air, the others were painfully pressed to the floor – then the father gave him a strong, ultimately saving push from behind, and he flew, bleeding heavily, far into his room. The door was slammed shut with the cane, and then it was quiet.

Mrs. Margarete Brigge, as far as I can recall, had always been a tall, inaccessible old woman. I cannot help but imagine that she was much older than the Chamberlain. She lived her life among us without considering anyone. She was not dependent on any of us and always had a sort of companion, an aging Countess Oxe, whom she had bound to herself through her generosity. This must have been an exception, as kindness was not her nature. She did not love children, and animals were not allowed near her. I don't know if she loved anything else. It was said that she had been engaged to the handsome Felix Lichnowski as a young girl, who then died so brutally in Frankfurt. Indeed, after her death, a portrait of the prince was there, which, if I'm not mistaken, was returned to the family. Perhaps, I think now, she missed out on something over this withdrawn country life that Ulsgaard's life had become year after year. It's hard to say if she mourned it. Perhaps she despised it because it had not come about, because it had missed the opportunity to live skillfully and talentedly. She had taken all of this so deeply into herself and had set up numerous, brittle, somewhat metallic-shining shells, each of which had a new and cool surface. Occasionally, however, she revealed herself through a naive impatience, not being paid enough attention; at my time, she could suddenly choke on something at the table in a clear and complicated way, which ensured the participation of all and made her, for a moment at least, as sensational and exciting as she might have been in the grand scheme of things. However, I suspect that my father was the only one who took these frequent occurrences seriously. He saw her, politely bent over, and you could tell that he offered her, in thought, his own ordinary windpipe, making it available for her. The Chamberlain, of course, had also stopped eating; he took a small sip of wine and kept his opinion to himself.

Lady Margarete Brigge had always seemed, as far as I can recall, a tall, inaccessible old woman. I cannot help but imagine that she was much older than the Chamberlain. She lived her life amongst us without considering anyone else. She was not reliant on any of us and always had a sort of companion, an aging Countess Oxe, whom she had bound to herself through her generosity. This must have been an exception, for generosity was not her nature. She did not love children, and animals were not allowed near her. I am not sure if she loved anything else. It was said that she had once been engaged to the handsome Felix Lichnowski, who then died so cruelly in Frankfurt. And indeed, a portrait of a prince was there after her death, which, I believe, was returned to the family. Perhaps, I think now, she missed out on another, more brilliant life over this confined rural life that life at Ulsgaard had become over the years. It is hard to say if she mourned it. Perhaps she despised it for having missed the opportunity to live skillfully and talentedly. She had taken all of this so deeply within herself and had set up many, brittle, slightly metallic gleaming shells, each of which its uppermost shell stood out anew and coolly. Fathers and teachers, I ponder: "What is hell?" I reason thus: "Suffering that one can no longer love." Once, in the infinite, unmeasurable existence, given to some spiritual being, with its appearance on earth, it was given the ability to say to itself: "I am, and I love." Only once was it given a moment of active, living love, but for that, earthly life, along with time and limits, was given. And what if this happy being rejected this invaluable gift, did not appreciate it, did not love, looked at it mockingly, and remained insensible? Such a being, already departed from the earth, sees Abraham's womb and speaks with Abraham, as it is indicated in the parable of the rich man and Lazarus, and sees heaven, and can ascend to God, but precisely because of this, and because it neglected the love it scorned, it torments itself. For I see clearly and tell myself: "Now I have knowledge, and though I desired to love, there will be no effort in my love, no sacrifice, for earthly life is over and there will be no more time!" Though I might have been willing to sacrifice my own life for others, but it is no longer possible, for that life, which could have been offered in sacrifice for love, has passed, and now there is an abyss between that life and this being. They speak of the material fire of hell: I do not investigate this mystery and fear it, but I think, if there were a material fire, then truly they would have rejoiced, for in material torment perhaps the most dreadful spiritual torment would have been forgotten for a moment. And it is impossible to take away their spiritual torment, for this torment is not external, but within them. If it were possible to take it away, I think, they would have become even more miserable. For though the righteous in heaven, observing their torments, would call them to themselves, loving infinitely, they would have only increased their torments, for they would have aroused in them even stronger the flame of the desire for a responsive, active, and grateful love, which is no longer possible. In the depths of my heart, I think, but alas, I cannot express this clearly. But woe to the self-destructors, woe to my brothers and others! I think that there is no one more wretched than them. Sin, they say, is unfit to pray to God for them, and the church seems to reject them on the outside, but in the secret of my soul, I think that it is possible to pray for them. For Christ will not be ashamed of love. I have inwardly prayed for such ones all my life, I confess this to you, fathers and teachers, and I still pray for them every day.

"My boat stops in the green water, foggy waves within,
In the remote mountains, vast and wild, I call home.
I love the stream and the bridge, where the spring waters rise,
And I cherish the cliffs and mornings, when the clouds are sparse.
The dragon gate is filled with fresh fish, cooked to savor,
And the insects and worms provide firewood, dried under the sun.
The fishing net is abundant, a reward for the aged,
The burden of two ropes, a task I can bear till the end.
I recline in my small boat, gazing at the flying geese,
I walk on the slanted paths, listening to the singing cranes.
My tongue and lips, the stage, where no distinction lies,
Right and wrong, the sea inside, holds few of my footprints.
Clothes hung to dry by the stream, like silk, they gleam,
Ax sharpened on the stones, like a blade, it gleams.
The autumn moon shines brightly, often alone I fish,
The spring mountains are quiet, no one I meet.
The fish are many, traded for wine to share with my spouse,
The firewood remains, filled to the brim, to quench the thirst of my descendants."

The dragon gate fresh fish is cooked, the insects and spiders dry the firewood daily. The fishing nets are numerous, can be a gift for the old, the ropes on the shoulders are two things, can be borne till the end. The small boat reclines, looking at the flying geese, the slanted pathway beckons, listening to the calling cranes. The mouth and tongue are in the stage, there is no me division, right or wrong in the sea, few are my footsteps. The streamside hangs the drying fabric like jade, the rocks are sharpened like a sword. Autumn moon shines bright, often alone fishing, spring mountains are quiet, no one meets. Many fish change wine, the same as the wife drinking, the remaining firewood is poured into the pot, the children share the jar. "

"Resting boat at the green water, where the fish and geese are numerous. The mountains and valleys are isolated, only the roaring brooks echo. The peak is sharp, the cloud is white, my thoughts are far away. I don't know when the evening mist will rise, when the sun will set, when the autumn moon will shine. The river water is clear, the fish is abundant, the mountains are green, the sky is vast. The moonlit night is silent, the mountain spring is cold, the stream is clear, the wild geese fly back and forth. The fisherman is in seclusion, he listens to the singing of the cranes, he speaks of the ancient poems, he dreams of the golden days."

Ancestor: "The character 'Dao' has three hundred and sixty side doors, each with a proper outcome. Which door are you studying?"
Tripitaka: "I follow your intention, master."
Ancestor: "I will teach you the 'Jiu' character's way, how about that?"
Tripitaka: "What is the way of the 'Jiu' character?"
Ancestor: "The 'Jiu' character's door houses certain practices such as summoning immortals, consulting turtles to divide the yarrow stalks, and discerning the principles of seeking good and avoiding misfortune."
Tripitaka: "Does it lead to longevity like this?"
Ancestor: "No! No!"
Tripitaka: "I will not study!"
