Aschenbach attempted to threaten him with his finger. "But I advise you, Kritobulos," he thought, smiling, "go on a year-long journey! For you need at least time for recovery." And then he ate large, ripe strawberries, which he bought from a vendor. It had become very warm, although the sun could not penetrate the misty layer of the sky. Lassitude held his spirit captive, while his senses enjoyed the incredible and stupefying entertainment of the stillness of the sea. To guess, to explore, what name it was that sounded something like "Adgio," seemed a suitable, completely engaging task and occupation for the serious man. And with the help of some Polish memories, he concluded that "Tadzio" must be meant, the abbreviation of "Tadeusz" and the diminutive form "Tadziu." Tadzio was bathing. Aschenbach, who had lost sight of him, spotted his head, his arm, which he was rowing out, far out in the sea; for the sea seemed shallow for a long way out. But already there seemed to be concern for him, already women's voices called for him from the huts, repeated this name, which almost ruled the beach like a solution and with its soft consonants, its drawn-out u-sound at the end, had something both sweet and wild: "Tadziu, Tadziu!" He obeyed, he ran, splashing the reluctant water with his legs, returning with a thrown-back head through the flood; and to see how the living figure, youthfully beautiful and harsh, emerged from the depths of heaven and sea, escaping and leaving the elements: This sight inspired mythical imaginations, it was like poetic knowledge from early times, from the origin of form and the birth of the gods. Aschenbach listened with closed eyes to this song echoing within him; and once again he thought, that it was good here and that he wanted to stay.

Monk: "A monk must be upright, and must bear hardships and suffering to become a disciple." Eight-fold Bodhisattva: "Brother, see how heavy this bundle of luggage is?" The Traveler replied: "Brother, ever since I have you and the monk, I have never complained about it, so how would I know how heavy it is?" Eight-fold Bodhisattva: "Brother, look at the count: four pieces of yellow vines, eight lengths of rope. We need to protect ourselves from rain and wind, with several layers of canvas. The bag itself is still slippery, and there are nails on both ends. The staff has nine rings of copper and iron. The big tent is woven with rattan and vines. This much luggage is hard for a wild boar to carry every day. Yet you became a disciple, and made me a laborer! " The Traveler laughed: "Fool, who did you say that to?" Eight-fold Bodhisattva: "Brother, I said that to you." The Traveler said: "You were wrong to say that to me. I only care about the teacher, but you and the monk, you're in charge of the luggage and horses. But if you slack off a little, you'll get a harsh whip first!"

The Great Saint, upon hearing the words, chuckled softly and said: "This Buddha is quite foolish! My descendant took a single step and journeyed ten million eight thousand li. How can he not leap over?!" With a loud voice, he asked: "If that is so, can you make such a claim?" The Buddha answered: "I can! I can!" He stretched out his right hand, appearing as small as a lily pad. The Great Saint grabbed the Vajra staff, shook it with divine might, straightened his body, and stood within the palm of the Buddha's hand, saying with a loud voice: "I shall leave too!" Indeed, he vanished, leaving only a trail of cloud light. The Buddha, with his enlightened gaze, observed the Monkey King, who was just like a whirling windmill, moving forward without ceasing. As the Great Saint traveled, he suddenly saw five flesh-colored pillars supporting a stream of green qi. He said: "This is indeed the end of the road. On my return, the Buddha will bear witness that the Spirit Hall is where I shall sit." He also considered: "Let me leave some markings here, it will be easier to converse with the Buddha." He plucked a single hair, blew upon it with divine breath, and called for it to "transform!" It transformed into a brush, double-tipped and ink-laden, and he wrote a large inscription on the central pillar: "The Great Saint, having made a journey here." He finished writing, retrieved the hair. Again, he did not act with reverence, but he scattered a pool of monkey urine at the base of the first pillar. He then turned the cloud-like staff upside-down and returned to his original location, standing again within the palm of the Buddha: "I have gone and have returned. Teach the Jade Emperor to grant the Heavenly Palace to me."

Then the Great Sage heard the words, and he smiled secretly, saying, "This Buddha is quite stupid! My monkey child traveled ten thousand eight hundred li. How can he not jump out?!" He shouted loudly, "If you say so, can you prove it?" The Buddha answered, "I can! I can!" He extended his right hand, which seemed as small as a lotus leaf. The Great Sage received the Ruyi Jingu Bang, shook it with divine power, extended his body, and stood within the palm of the Buddha's hand, saying loudly, "I will also leave!" You see him travel with a cloud of light, leaving no trace. The Buddha's wise eyes watched, seeing that the Monkey King resembled a windmill that could not stop, only moving forward. On my way back, the Buddha will provide evidence, and the Spirit Palace will certainly be mine to sit on." He also thought to himself, "I must wait! It transformed into a brush with thick ink and double goose feathers. He wrote a large cloud-like characters in the middle of the columns, saying, "The Great Sage Equal to Heaven, visited here once." He finished, then put away the hair. He did not show respect, but under the root of the first column, he scattered a puddle of monkey urine. He turned the cloud into a turbine, returned to his original location, and stood in the palm of the Buddha's hand, saying, "I have left, and now I have returned. Teach the Jade Emperor to let the Heavenly Palace meet me."

However, she stripped him of his feathers and horns, took off the jeweled collar around his neck, and only then did he transform into this horse. He wished to carry his master westward to pay homage to the Buddha. This is all the result of individual merit; do not envy him. When the sand monk heard this, he asked, "Brother, is he a dragon?" The traveler replied, "He is a dragon." Eight Bull Demon asked, "Brother, I have heard it said that dragons can spout clouds and mist, scatter earth and sand. With their skills of flipping over mountains and stirring up seas, why is he walking so slowly today?" The traveler replied, "If you want him to walk faster, I can make him go faster. Try it and see." The Great Sage, holding the Iron Staff, began to whirl it around, and a thousand colors of clouds formed. The horse, seeing the staff, was terrified it would be struck and panicked, running off at the speed of lightning. For several years, the Indian cholera had shown a heightened propensity for spreading and wandering. Originating from the warm morasses of the Ganges Delta, it rose up with the noxious vapors of that lush, uninhabitable, human-avoided primordial and island wilderness, in whose bamboo thickets the tiger lurks, it had ravaged all of India continuously and unusually fiercely, spreading eastward to China, westward to Afghanistan and Persia, and, following the main caravan routes, spreading its terror as far as Astrakhan, yes, even to Moscow. However, while Europe trembled, fearing that the specter would cross the land and sea, it was, carried by Syrian merchants across the sea, almost simultaneously detected in several Mediterranean ports, it raised its head in Toulon and Malaga, showed its face in Palermo and Naples multiple times and seemed unwilling to retreat from all of Calabria and Apulia. The northern part of the peninsula had been spared. However, in mid-May of this year, cholera vibrions were found in the emaciated, black bodies of a sailor and a greenware dealer in Venice. The cases were hushed up. But after a week, there were ten, twenty, thirty, and these in various districts. A man from the Austrian province, who had stayed for pleasure in Venice for a few days, died, returning to his hometown, under undeniable symptoms, and so it came to pass that the first rumors of the scourge of the Lagoon City reached German daily newspapers. Venice's authorities responded that the health conditions of the city had never been better and took the necessary measures to combat it. However, it is likely that the food supplies had been contaminated. Vegetables, meat, or milk, for lying and covering up, death spread in the narrow alleys around the canals, and the early summer heat, which warmed the water of the canals, was particularly conducive to its spread. It seemed as if the disease had renewed its strength, as if the tenacity and fertility of its agents had doubled. Cases of recovery were very rare; eighty out of a hundred of the infected died, and in a terrifying way, for the evil appeared with extreme ferocity and often showed its most dangerous form, which is called "the dry." Here, the body could not even expel the massively secreted water. Within a few hours, the sick person would wither and choke on the thickened blood, writhing in convulsions and feverish cries. If, as sometimes happened, the outbreak followed a brief illness in the form of a deep coma from which he did not wake up, the authorities were alarmed. In early June, the isolation barracks of the Civic Hospital and the two orphanages were filling up in silence, and a frantic traffic was taking place between the quay of the new foundations and San Michele, the cemetery island. But fear of general damage, consideration for the recently opened art exhibition in the public gardens, fear of massive losses, in the event of panic and scandal, for the hotels, businesses, and the entire diverse foreign trade, was stronger in the city than truthfulness and respect for international agreements; it managed to keep the authorities' policy of silence and denial obstinate. The top medical official of Venice, a deserving man, was displeased with his post and had resigned and been replaced by a more pliable person under the table. The people knew this; and the corruption of the ruling classes, combined with the prevailing uncertainty, the state of emergency in which the immediate death of the city immersed it, brought about a certain depravity in the lower classes, an encouragement of shy and antisocial impulses, which manifested itself in insubordination, shamelessness, and increasing criminality. Disregarding the rules, one noticed many drunkards in the evenings; malicious elements made the streets dangerous at night; robberies and even murder attempts were repeated, for it had been proven that supposed victims of the cholera had in fact been removed from life by their own relatives with poison; and commercial immorality took aggressive and debauched forms, as they were not usually known here and were only familiar in the south of the country and in the East.

He listened for a long time. Somewhere far away, below, possibly outside the gates, two voices could be heard, arguing and fighting loudly. "Who are they...?" He waited patiently. Suddenly, everything grew silent, as if cut off; they dispersed. He wanted to go out, but then a door at the lower level burst open with a noise, and someone began to descend the stairs, humming a tune. "How can they be so noisy!" – a thought flashed through his mind. He again feigned a closed door and waited it out. Suddenly, everything grew quiet, not a breath. He had already taken a step onto the stairs, when suddenly new steps could be heard again.

Already cavalier, as he always did, he emerged from under the table and ran toward her. I saw it, Malte, I saw it. He ran toward her, though she did not come; for him, she did. We understood that he was running toward her. Twice he glanced at us, as if he were asking. Then he rushed at her, as always, Malte, exactly as always, and reached her; for he began to jump around her, Malte, in search of something that was not there, and then up at her, to lick her, straight up. We heard him whine with joy, and how he flew so quickly, multiple times rapidly in succession, one could have truly believed that he would mark her with his leaps. But suddenly he began to howl, and he spun around in mid-air from his own momentum and fell back, strangely awkwardly, and lay quite peculiarly flat there and did not move. From the other side, the servant came out of the house with the letters. He hesitated for a while; apparently, it was not entirely easy for him to approach our faces. And your father nodded for him to stay. Your father, Malte, loved no animals; but now he did indeed go, slowly as it seemed to me, and bent over the dog. He said something to the servant, something short, monosyllabic. I saw how the servant jumped up to lift Cavalier. But your father himself took the animal and went into the house with it, as if he knew exactly where to go.

Someone must have defamed Joseph K., for he had done nothing wrong when he was arrested one morning. The cook of Mrs. Grubach, his landlady, who usually brought him breakfast at eight every morning, did not come this time. This had never happened before. K. waited a while, looking out from his pillow at the old woman who lived across from him and watched him with an unusual eagerness, then, both surprised and hungry, he rang the bell. Immediately, someone knocked, and a man entered whom K. had never seen in this apartment before. He was thin but solidly built, wearing a tight black suit, which was adorned with various folds, pockets, fasteners, buttons, and a belt, making it appear practical without it being immediately clear what its purpose was. "Who are you?" K asked, sitting up half in bed. The man, however, passed over the question as if it were not important and simply said, "Did you ring?" "Anna should bring me breakfast," K replied, trying to figure out who the man really was by paying close attention and thinking it over. But this man did not linger under his gaze, instead turning to the door, which he opened slightly to say to someone who was apparently standing just behind the door, "He wants Anna to bring him breakfast." A soft laughter came from the next room, it was not clear whether more than one person were involved. Although the stranger did not learn anything new from this, he told K in a tone of announcement, "It is impossible." "That would be new," K said, jumped out of bed and quickly pulled on his pants. "I want to see who is in the next room and how Mrs. Grubach will explain this disturbance to me." It occurred to him that he did not have to say this aloud, and by doing so he was in a way acknowledging the stranger's right to supervise him, but it seemed unimportant to him now. In fact, the stranger reacted as if this were the case, for he said, "Would you rather stay here?" "I don't want to stay here, nor do I want to be addressed by you, as long as you don't identify yourself." "It was well-intentioned," the stranger said and opened the door freely. K slowly entered the next room, where it looked almost exactly the same as the night before. It was Mrs. Grubach's living room, filled with furniture, fabrics, porcelain, and photographs. There was perhaps a little more room in this overfilled room today, but it was hard to tell. The main change was the presence of a man sitting at the open window with a book in his hand, looking up from it now. "You should have stayed in your room! Didn't Franz tell you?" "What do you want?" K asked, looking from the new acquaintance to the man standing in the doorway and then back. Through the open window, he saw the old woman again, who had come to the window across from him to watch as well. "I want to see Mrs. Grubach," K said, made a motion as if he were trying to separate himself from the two men, but they were far from him. "No," the man by the window said, threw the book on a small table, and stood up. "You are not allowed to leave, you have been arrested." "It looks like that," K said. "And why then?" he asked then. "We are not authorized to tell you. Wait in your room and wait. The proceedings have been initiated, and you will find out everything in due time. I am going beyond my mission if I tell you this in a friendly manner. But I hope it will only be Franz who hears it, and he is himself always friendly to you. If you are as lucky as you were with the choice of your guards, then you can be optimistic." K wanted to sit down, but he saw that there was no seat in the entire room except for the chair by the window. "You will see how right it all is," Franz said, and went out with the other man. The latter man, who was much taller than K, patted him on the shoulder several times. Both checked K's nightshirt and said that he would now have to wear a much worse shirt, but they would keep his other clothes and, if his case turned out favorably, return them to him. "It is better if you give the things to us as collateral," they said, "because there are often irregularities in the depository, and in addition, everything is sold there after a certain time, regardless of whether the corresponding case is still open or not. And how long do these proceedings usually take, especially lately! You will eventually, however, receive the deposit's earnings, but this earnings is, firstly, small in itself, secondly, it is determined not by the offer, but by the bribe, and furthermore, such earnings are, according to experience, reduced by a factor of 10 whenever they are passed on from hand to hand and from year to year." K paid little attention to these speeches, the right to dispose of his things, which he may still have possessed, was of little value to him, much more important to him was to get clarity about his situation; in the presence of these people, however, he could not even think, for the stomach of the second guard - it could only have been guards - pressed against him comfortably, he looked up, but he saw a dry, brittle, bony face with a strongly twisted nose, which communicated with the other guard. What kind of people were these? What were they talking about? To what authority did they belong? K lived in a state governed by law, peace reigned everywhere, all laws were enforced, who would dare to storm his apartment? He was inclined to accept everything as easily as possible, to only believe the worst when the worst actually happened, to make no preparations for the future, even if everything threatened him. Here, however, it seemed to him that this was not right, one could certainly see it as a joke, a crude joke, which his colleagues at the bank might have organized for unknown reasons, perhaps because today was his thirtieth birthday - but still, he was determined this time, from the very first sight of guard Franz, not to give up any advantage he may have had over these people. In the fact that later it would be said that he had not understood the joke, he saw a very small danger, but he remembered - without this being his usual habit, learning from experience - some insignificant cases, in which he had acted unthinkingly, and been punished for it. It should not happen again, at least not this time; was it a comedy, he wanted to play along.

At the start of the process, Mother Raskolnikov fell ill. Dunya and Razumihin found it possible to take her out of St. Petersburg during the entire trial. Razumihin chose a city on the railroad and close to St. Petersburg so that he could regularly monitor all aspects of the trial and, at the same time, frequently see Avdotya Romanovna. Pulcheria Alexandrovna's illness was strange, nervous, and accompanied by something akin to madness, if not entirely, then at least partially. Upon returning from her last meeting with her brother, Dunya found her mother already very ill, with a fever and delirium. On the same evening, she conspired with Razumihin about what to tell her mother about her brother, and even invented, together with him, a whole story about Raskolnikov's sudden departure far away, to the Russian border, on a single private assignment, which would eventually bring him both money and fame. However, they were surprised that Pulcheria Alexandrovna neither asked about it then nor later. On the contrary, she had her own story about her son's sudden departure; she told it with tears, implying that many important and mysterious circumstances were known only to her and that Rodion had many very strong enemies, so he even had to hide. As for his future career, she also considered it undeniable and brilliant, when certain unfavorable circumstances passed; she assured Razumihin that her son would eventually become a man of state, which was evident from his article and his brilliant literary talent. She read this article continuously, sometimes even out loud, almost slept with it, but almost never asked where Rody was now, despite the fact that, apparently, they avoided talking about this with her, which could already have fueled her delusion. They finally began to fear this strange silence about certain points from Pulcheria Alexandrovna. For example, she didn't even complain about the lack of letters from him, although, living in her own village, she had lived only on the hope and expectation of receiving a letter from her beloved Rody sooner. This last circumstance was too inexplicable and greatly worried Dunya; she often thought that her mother, perhaps, foreboded something terrible in her son's fate and was afraid to ask to avoid learning something even more terrible. In any case, Dunya clearly saw that Pulcheria Alexandrovna was not in a sound state of mind.

Note: The word "Aglea" in the original refers to a character in the story and should be translated as Aglea in the English translation. Also, the word "kopeck" is a Russian unit of currency, and the number "sixty" should be written as "60" in English.

I enclosed six rubles in the letter, sealed it, and implored Apollo to deliver it to Simov. Upon learning that there was money in the letter, Apollo became more respectful and agreed to go. By evening, I stepped out for a walk. My head still ached and spun from the previous day. As the evening approached and the twilight thickened, my impressions and thoughts grew more unstable and confusing. Something refused to die within me, deep in my heart and conscience, unwilling to perish and burning with keen longing. I wandered more on the most populated, industrial streets, on Meschansky, on Sadovaya, near Yusupov's garden. I always enjoyed strolling along these streets in twilight, especially when there was a crowd of every passerby, industrial and artisanal, with faces full of concern, dispersing to their homes after a day's work. I particularly liked this money-driven hustle and bustle, this blatant prosaism. This time, all this street noise irritated me even more. I couldn't control myself, couldn't find an end. Something rose, rose incessantly in my soul with pain, and refused to subside. Completely distraught, I returned home. It was as if some crime lay on my conscience.

K. was startled by a call from the adjacent room so much that he knocked his teeth against the glass. "The supervisor is calling for you!" it said. What terrified him was just the screaming, that brief, hacked, military screaming that he never would have believed from the guard Franz. The command itself was welcome. "At last!" he exclaimed, closed the wardrobe and rushed immediately into the adjacent room. There stood the two guards and chased him, as if it was self-evident, back into his room. "What's the matter with you?" they called. "Want to face the supervisor in your undershirt? He'll have you beaten up and us too!" "Let me, damn it!" K. shouted, backed up against his wardrobe, "if they catch me in bed, can't they expect to find me in formal attire." "It doesn't help" the guards said, who always, when K. shouted, remained calm, almost sad, and thus confused or brought him to his senses. "Ridiculous ceremonies!" he growled, but already picked up a suit jacket from the chair and held it for a moment with both hands, as he presented it to the judgment of the guards. They shook their heads. "It must be a black suit" they said. K. threw the suit jacket to the floor and said - he didn't know what he meant by it -: "It's not even the main trial yet." The guards laughed, but remained firm in their: "It must be a black suit." "If I speed up the process, it should be allowed" K. said, opened the wardrobe himself, searched for a long time among the many clothes, selected his best black suit, a jacket suit that had almost made an impression among his acquaintances, took out another shirt and began to dress carefully. In secret, he believed he had managed to accelerate the whole thing by making the guards forget about making him take a bath. He observed them, whether they might remember it, but that didn't even occur to them, on the contrary, Willem didn't forget to send Franz with the message that K. was getting dressed to the supervisor.

Here, Ippolit Kirillovich unfolded the entire picture of the fatal passion of the accused towards Gryusha. He began with the very moment when the accused went to see the "young woman" in order to "beat her," as the accused himself expressed it, Ippolit Kirillovich explained, "but instead of beating her, he remained at her feet – that was the beginning of this love. At the same time, the old man, the accused's father, casts his gaze on the same woman – a coincidence that is both surprising and fatal, for both hearts suddenly flared up at the same time, although both he and the other had known and encountered this woman before – and both these hearts flared up with the most uncontrollable, the most Dostoevsky-like passion. Here we have her own admission: "I laughed at both of them". Yes, she wanted to suddenly laugh at both of them; she had not wanted to before, but suddenly that intention occurred to her, and it ended with both of them falling before her, defeated. The old man, who worshiped money as if it were God, prepared three thousand rubles immediately just for her to visit his home, but soon he was driven to the point where he would have been willing to put his own name and all his fortune at her feet, as long as she agreed to become his lawful wife. We have strong evidence for this. As for the accused, his tragedy is obvious, it is before us. But this was the "game" of the young woman. The unfortunate young man was not given even the hope, for real hope was given to him only in the very last moment, when he, kneeling before his tormentor, extended to her already bloodied hands, those of his father and his rival: it was in this position that he was arrested. "Send me, send me to Siberia along with him, I drove him to it, I am the most guilty!" – this woman herself exclaimed, already in sincere repentance, at the moment of his arrest. The talented young man who took on the task of describing the actual case – Mr. Rakitin, whom I have already mentioned – defines the character of this heroine in a few compressed and characterizing phrases: "Early disappointment, early deception and fall, betrayal of the fiancé who left her, poverty, the curse of an honest family, and finally, the patronage of one rich old man, whom she, of course, now considers her benefactor. In the young heart, which may have contained much goodness, anger smoldered from too early a time. A calculating character developed, accumulating capital. A mocking and vengeful attitude towards society developed." After this characterization, it is clear that she could laugh at both of them only for the sake of a game, for a malicious game. And here in this month of desperate love, moral fall, betrayal of her fiancé, misappropriation of someone else's money entrusted to his honor, the accused, in addition, approaches madness, almost madness, from continuous jealousy, and to whom but to his father! And the main thing, the mad old man tempted and seduced the object of his passion – these very same three thousand rubles, which the son considers his family's inheritance, the property of his mother, in which he reproaches his father. Yes, I agree, it was hard to bear! Here madness could have appeared. It was not about the money, but about the fact that this money was being destroyed with such offensive cynicism, happiness!"

I ran after him and started shouting; but since I had nothing else to shout but "Hey!", he didn't turn around. Suddenly, he ducked to the left, into the gate of one house. When I ran through the gate, it was very dark under it, and already nobody was there. The house was of enormous size, one of those "village" houses that are built by speculators for small apartments; in other such houses, there are numbers up to a hundred. When I ran through the gate, it seemed to me that a person was walking in the right, rear corner of the enormous courtyard, although in the darkness I could hardly make out anything. I ran up to the corner and saw the entrance to the staircase; the staircase was narrow, very dirty, and not well lit; but I could hear someone climbing the stairs higher up, and I ran up the staircase, counting on the fact that, at some point, he would rest, and I would catch up to him. And so it happened. The stairs were too short, the number was infinite, so I got very winded; the door was opened and closed again on the fifth floor, I could tell that even three floors below. While I was panting and catching my breath on the landing, looking for a bell, several minutes passed. Finally, an old woman opened the door for me, who was puffing up a samovar in a tiny kitchen; she listened to my silent questions, of course, understood nothing, and silently opened the door to the next room, also small and very low, with shabby necessary furniture and a wide, huge bed under the drapes, on which lay "Terentych" (that's what the old woman called him), I thought he was drunk. On the table, a fire was burning in an iron crib and a half-empty shirt lay standing. Terentych muttered something to me lying down and waved me to the next door, and the old woman left, so I had no choice but to open that door. I did so and entered the next room.

He walked along the long and narrow corridor for a long time, finding no one, and was about to shout loudly, when suddenly in the dark corner, between an old cabinet and a door, he saw a strange object, something that seemed alive. He leaned forward with the candle and saw a child - a girl no older than five, in a tattered, ragged dress, shaking and crying. She seemed not to be frightened of Svidrigailov, but looked at him with bewildered, large, black eyes and occasionally gasped, like children who have been crying for a long time but have already stopped and even calmed down, yet still suddenly gasp. The girl's face was pale and exhausted; she had grown stiff from the cold, but "how did she end up here? It means she hid here and didn't sleep all night." He began to question her. The girl suddenly came to life and spoke quickly, rapidly babbling something in her childish language. There was something about "mama" and that "mama is limping", about some cup that was "broken" (smashed). The girl spoke without stopping; it was possible to guess from all these stories that this was an unwanted child, whom the mother, some perpetually drunk cook, probably from this very hotel, had beaten and terrorized; that the girl had broken her mother's cup and was so afraid that she fled even in the evening; she had probably hidden somewhere on the porch, in the rain, until she finally made it here, hid behind the cabinet and spent the night here in the corner, crying, trembling from dampness, darkness, and fear, afraid that she would now be punished for all this. He picked her up, went to his room, sat her on the bed, and began to undress her. Her damp slippers, on her bare foot, were as wet as if they had lain in a puddle all night. After undressing, he put her in bed, covered her, and completely wrapped her up in a blanket. She immediately fell asleep. After finishing, he again fell into a brooding silence.

An hour passed before she appeared. They had arrived and yet she was not; they were not in a hurry, but they felt restless. The young Poles, dressed patriotically and perhaps influenced by the military trumpet signals echoing from the public gardens across the water, had come on deck, and, intoxicated by the Asti, they raised a cheer for the Bersaglieri exercising on the other side. But it was disheartening to see the state the elderly man had been brought to by his false camaraderie with the youth. His old brain had not been able to withstand the wine, he was pitifully drunk. Dazed eyes, a cigarette hanging between trembling fingers, he wavered, struggling to maintain his balance, standing still, pulled forward and back by the intoxication. He almost fell, but he dared not move from the spot, yet he displayed a pathetic arrogance, clinging to anyone who approached him, babbling, winking, chuckling, waving his gnarled, wrinkled finger in a foolish gesture, and leering obscenely with his tongue at the corners of his mouth. Aschenbach looked at him with darkening brows, and again a feeling of numbness came over him, as if the world showed a slight, but irresistible tendency to degenerate into the bizarre and grotesque; a feeling that was, however, held back by the circumstances, as the thumping activity of the machine began anew and the ship resumed its interrupted journey through the San Marco Canal. So he saw him again, the most surprising landing place, that brilliant composition of a fantastic building, which the Republic presented to the reverent gazes of approaching seafarers: the light grandeur of the palace and the groaning bridge, the columns with lions and saints on the shore, the ostentatious front of the fairy-tale temple, the glimpse of alley and giant clock, and as he looked, he remembered that on land, at the station in Venice, one entered a palace through a back door, and that one could reach the most unlikely of cities only by sea, as across a lofty ocean.

Pain did not abate; but Ivan Illyich made efforts to convince himself that he was getting better. He could deceive himself as long as nothing disturbed him. However, whenever there was a problem with his wife, a setback at work, or bad cards in a game, he felt the full force of his disease; sometimes he bore these setbacks, hoping that things would improve, that he would correct his mistakes, win, and succeed. Now every setback was a blow to him and plunged him into despair. He told himself that he was just starting to get better and the medicine was beginning to work, and then this damned misfortune or trouble... He was angry at the misfortune or those causing him trouble and felt how his anger was killing him, but could not restrain himself. It seemed to him that he should be aware that his anger was intensifying his disease and that he should therefore ignore the unfortunate incidents; but he made the opposite conclusion: he thought he needed calm, paid attention to everything that disrupted his calm, and became enraged at any minor disruption. His situation worsened because he read medical books and consulted doctors. The worsening was gradual, so that he could deceive himself by comparing one day with another, there was little difference. However, when he consulted doctors, he felt that things were getting worse and very quickly at that. And yet, he continued to consult doctors.

Monk is a Tang Dynasty envoy sent to pay respects to Buddha in the West Heavens. Along the way, he encountered some wolves, tigers, snakes, and insects, which surrounded him and prevented him from moving forward. Suddenly, the Imperial Guard appeared, and all the animals scattered, saving the monk's life. Thank you! Thank you! Imperial Guard said: "I live here, subsisting by hunting wolves and tigers for a living and catching snakes and insects for survival. That's why all these animals are afraid of me and have left. As you are a Tang Dynasty envoy, we are both countrymen. This place is still within the borders of the Tang Dynasty, and I, too, am a commoner of the Tang Dynasty. We share the same water and soil as the emperor, indeed, we are all citizens of one country. You need not fear, come with me, rest your horses at my abode, and I will escort you on your journey in the morning." Monk, overjoyed, thanked the Imperial Guard and led his horses to follow.

If the wickedness of man provokes you with unbearable anger and irrepressible sorrow, even to the point of desiring revenge upon the wicked, then fear this feeling above all; immediately go and find suffering for yourself as if you were guilty of the wickedness of man. Accept these sufferings and endure, and your heart will be pacified, and you will understand that you too are guilty, for you could have shone as a spotless one and did not. Had you shone, you would have illuminated another way, and the one who committed wickedness might not have done so in your light. Even if you did shine, but you see that people are not saved, not even in your light, then remain firm and do not doubt the power of heavenly light; believe that if they are not saved now, they will be saved later. And if they are not saved later, then the children of theirs will be saved, for your light will not die, even if you have already died. The righteous depart, but their light remains. Those who are always saved are saved only after the one who is saving has died. The human race does not accept its prophets and persecutes them, but the people love their martyrs and honor those who were tortured. You, however, work for the good of all, and for the future you labor. Do not seek rewards, for the reward you already have is great on this earth: the spiritual joy that only the righteous attain. Do not fear the noble or the strong, but be wise and always act with dignity. Know the measure, know the time, learn this. In solitude, pray. Love to fall prostrate upon the earth and kiss it. Kiss the earth and never cease, never tire of loving, love all, love everyone, seek ecstasy and frenzy in this. Bathe the earth in tears of joy and love these tears of yours. Do not be ashamed of this ecstasy, cherish it, for it is a gift from God, a great one, and it is not given to many, but to the chosen few.

Petr Ivanovich sighed even more deeply and sorrowfully, and Praxina Fedorovna thanked him graciously by shaking his hand. Entering her lavish rose-colored chinoiserie room with a dim lamplight, they sat down at the table: she on the sofa, and Petr Ivanovich on a sagging spring and improperly placed low ottoman. Praxina Fedorovna wanted to warn him to sit on another chair, but found this warning inappropriate for her position and reconsidered. Sitting on this ottoman, Petr Ivanovich remembered how Ivan Ilyich had arranged this room and consulted with him about the very same rose-colored one with green leaves chinoiserie. Sitting on the sofa and passing by the table (in fact, the entire room was filled with knick-knacks and furniture), the widow snagged the black lace of her black shawl on the table's carving. Petr Ivanovich rose to free it, and the ottoman, now freed, began to tremble and push him. The widow herself began to free her lace, and Petr Ivanovich sat down again, squashing the rebellious ottoman. However, the widow did not completely free it, and Petr Ivanovich rose again, and the ottoman began to rebel again and even clicked. When all of this ended, she pulled out a clean batiste handkerchief and began to cry. The incident with the lace and the struggle with the ottoman cooled Petr Ivanovich, and he sat down stiffly. This awkward situation was interrupted by Sokolov, the butler of Ivan Ilyich, with a report that the plot of land on the cemetery, which Praxina Fedorovna had selected, would cost two hundred rubles. She stopped crying and, with the appearance of a sacrifice, looked at Petr Ivanovich and said in French that she was very troubled. Petr Ivanovich made a silent nod, expressing undeniable certainty that this could not be otherwise.

In the warm sunlight, mandarin ducks slept on the sandbanks, and butterflies flitted among the blooming flowers in the ravines. As autumn receded and winter dwindled, spring was half over, and it was unclear when this traveler would complete his true journey according to the scriptures. After traveling for five or seven days on desolate roads, they suddenly saw a village in the distance on the horizon. Sanzang said, "Monkey, look at that walled cottage nearby. It seems like a mountain monastery. Let's stop there and spend a night before continuing our journey tomorrow." The traveler said, "Let me first check the auspicious signs, then we can decide on our course." That master tugged at the reins of his white horse, and the traveler fixed his gaze, truly seeing: the woven bamboo fence was dense, and the thatched cottage was solid. Trees and shrubs loomed at the entrance, and a curved bridge spanned a clear stream that flowed under the eaves. Willows grew along the path, and fragrant flowers bloomed in the garden, releasing a fragrant aroma. At this time, the sun was setting in the west, and everywhere in the mountains and forests, birds were chirping noisily. The smoke rising from the chimneys filled the air, and the twisting roads were dotted with cattle and sheep. Again, Monkey saw that the chickens and pigs were well-fed and sleeping on the roof, and the neighbor was singing drunkenly. The traveler looked on and said, "Let's go, Master. This seems to be a good villager's home, and we can stay here for the night." That elder hurried the white horse and arrived at the street corner. They also saw a young man with his head wrapped in a cloth, wearing blue robes, carrying an umbrella and a backpack, wearing a loose belt and pants, and wearing a pair of three-legged shoes. Monkey reached out and pulled him by the arm, asking, "Where are you going? I'll ask you a question: What is the name of this place?" That person only struggled and shouted angrily, "I live alone on the farm, and I only want to send a message. Why are you bothering me?" Monkey smiled and said, "Don't be upset, it's more convenient for people to communicate. Just tell me the name of this place, and I can help you solve your problem." That person could not free himself from Monkey's grasp, and he was angry and jumped around. That place twisted his arm like an iron shovel, and he lost his bag, dropped his umbrella, and both of his hands were rain-soaked, as if they were trying to catch Monkey. Monkey supported his luggage with one hand and held the other hand, struggling to support himself. Monkey became more and more unwilling to let go, and he became more and more agitated, until he exploded with anger like thunder. Sanzang said, "Monkey, is there no one there? Why are you still holding onto him? Let him go." Monkey smiled and said, "Master, it's not that there's no one there. It's only that he's the one I should talk to. There's a transaction involved." That person was forced to tell the truth by Monkey, and he said, "This is the border of the Usu Kingdom, called High Old Village. Half the residents of the village have the surname High, so it's called High Old Village. You can let me go now." Monkey also said, "You don't look like someone from a nearby village. You should tell me where you are going and what you are planning to do. I'll only let you go after I hear your explanation." That person had no choice but to reveal his true intentions, saying, "I am High Tai-gong's family member, named High Cai. My grandfather has a daughter who is about twenty years old and has never married. Three years ago, a demon spirit possessed her. My grandfather was unhappy, saying that his daughter had invited the demon spirit, ruining the family's reputation, and preventing other relatives from visiting. The demon spirit refused to leave, and he kept my grandmother locked up in his backyard, and she hasn't been seen by the family for half a year. My grandfather gave me several silver coins and asked me to find a monk to exorcise the demon spirit. I have been traveling for a long time without rest, and I have asked several monks, but they all failed. Just now, I scolded you angrily, and I gave you five silver coins as a bribe, asking you to find a good monk to exorcise the demon spirit. I didn't expect to run into you, and I was mistaken, causing me to suffer here and there, so I called out to you. I didn't expect you to have some skill, and I couldn't escape your grasp, so I had to tell you the truth." Monkey said, "Your destiny and mine have come together. You don't need to waste money. We're not those incompetent monks and unclean Taoist priests. We actually have some techniques for exorcising demons. This is also a chance to fulfill our mission of escorting the dragon king and curing my blindness. You should go back and tell your grandpa that we are envoys from the East and are coming to the West to bow to Buddha and seek scriptures. We are skilled at exorcising demons and curing evil spirits." High Cai said, "Don't mislead me. I'm a hot-tempered person, and if you can't exorcise the demon spirit, not only will you not help me, but you will also cause me unnecessary trouble." Monkey said, "Don't worry, I won't mislead you. Lead me to your grandpa's door and wait for me to handle it." That person had no choice but to pick up his bag and umbrella again, turn around, and lead Sanzang and Monkey to the door of his grandpa's house and said, "Elders, please wait for a moment on the horse platform while I go in and report to the master of the house." Sanzang and Monkey only relaxed their hands after that, dismounted, and waited by the door.

Master opened the garden, shared and ate two, leaving twenty-eight; just now, two were beaten and shared with Tang Sage, leaving twenty-six; now there remain twenty-two, yet four more are left? Isn't it because those wicked people stole them? We should only blame Tang Sage for coming and going." Two of them stepped out of the garden and rushed to the palace, pointing at Tang Sage, bald on the head and back, vulgar in speech and abusive in words without cease; a thief's head and a mouse's brain, a foul-mouthed and ill-tempered scold. Tang Sage could not endure the words and said, "Spirit Child, what are you making a fuss about? Calm down a little, if you have something to say, say it slowly, don't scatter empty words." Clever Wind said, "You are deaf? I am speaking coarsely, and you don't understand? You stole and ate the ginseng persimmons, and you won't let me say anything about it." Tang Sage said, "What does a ginseng persimmon look like?" Bright Moon said, "I just brought it to eat with you, aren't they like a child's sweetmeats?" Tang Sage said, "Amitabha! As soon as I saw that thing, I was startled and my heart was in turmoil, yet I dare steal and eat it! Even if I am hungry, I dare not commit such a robbery."

It's just that I couldn't resist the temptation, but I wouldn't dare to commit this theft."

This orderly presentation initially astonished K., then, however, he whispered just as softly as the painter, "I think you contradict yourselves." "In what way?" the painter asked patiently and leaned back with a smile. This smile caused a feeling in K. that he was now attempting to discover contradictions not in the words of the painter, but in the proceedings themselves. However, he did not back down and said, "You earlier stated that the court is inaccessible for evidence, later you restricted this to the public court, and now you even say that the innocent need no help before the court. There is already a contradiction here. Furthermore, but earlier you also said that one can influence the judges personally, yet now you deny that the actual acquittal, as you call it, can ever be achieved through personal influence. There is another contradiction here." "These contradictions can easily be explained," said the painter. "Here we are speaking of two different things, what is written in the law, and what I have personally experienced. You must not confuse the two." "That is sufficient," said K., speaking to himself and his hopes. "Or have you heard of acquittals from earlier times?" "Acquittals," answered the painter, "there probably have been some. However, it is very difficult to determine this. The final decisions of the court are not published, they are not even accessible to the judges themselves, as a result, only legends have survived regarding old court cases. These contain, however, in the majority, actual acquittals, they can be believed, but they cannot be proven. However, they should not be completely ignored, they probably contain a certain truth, and they are also very beautiful. I myself have painted some pictures with these legends as their subject." "Merely legends do not change my opinion," said K., "can one not appeal to these legends in court?" The painter laughed. "No, that is not possible," he said. "Then it is pointless to discuss it," said K., he wanted to provisionally accept all the opinions of the painter, even though he found them unlikely and they contradicted other reports. He had now no time to check everything the painter said, or even to refute it, it was already the limit of his patience, if he managed to get the painter to help him in some way, even in a non-decisive way. That is why he said, "Let us then leave aside the actual acquittal. You mentioned two other possibilities." "The feigned acquittal and the abduction. It may only be the latter," said the painter. "Shall we not discuss that first?" asked K. The painter shrugged his shoulders and said, "Shall I not take off my coat first? It is quite warm." "Yes," said K., who until now had only paid attention to the explanations of the painter, but now, when he was reminded of the heat, sweat broke out heavily on his forehead. "It is almost unbearable." The painter nodded, as if he understood K.'s discomfort very well. "Can't the window be opened?" asked K. "No," said the painter. "It is just a fixed glass pane, it cannot be opened." Now K. realized that he had hoped all along that the painter or he himself would go to the window and smash it. He was prepared to swallow the fog with an open mouth. The feeling of being completely cut off from the air caused him to feel dizzy. He slapped lightly with his hand on the feather bed next to him and said with a weak voice, "This is uncomfortable and unhealthy." "Oh no," said the painter in defense of his window, "on the contrary, because it cannot be opened, it keeps the heat in here better than a double window. If I want to ventilate, I can open one or even both of my doors." K., reassured by this explanation, looked around to find the other door. The painter noticed this and said, "It is behind you, I had to put it beside the bed. "It is still too small for an atelier here," said the painter, as if trying to forestall any criticism from K. "I had to arrange it as best I could. The bed beside the door is, of course, in a very unfavorable position. The judge I am now painting, for example, always comes through the door beside the bed, and I have also given him a key to this door, so that he, even when I am not at home, can wait for me here in the atelier. Usually he comes early in the morning, while I am still sleeping. It always wakes me up, when the door beside the bed opens. I can never help but curse him when he steps over my bed in the morning. I could take away the key, but that would only make matters worse. One can break all the doors here with the least effort." During this entire speech, K. considered whether he should take off his coat, but he finally realized that if he did not, he would not be able to stay here any longer, so he took off his coat and laid it over his knees, so that he could put it back on if the conversation ended. As soon as he had taken off his coat, one of the girls called out, "He has already taken off his coat!" and one could hear how they pressed towards the cracks to see the spectacle. "The girls believe, you know," said the painter, "that I am going to paint you and that is why they undress." "So," said K., hardly amused, because he felt no better than before, even though he now wore shirt sleeves. Almost grumpily he asked, "What were the other two possibilities you mentioned?" He had already forgotten the terms. "The feigned acquittal and the abduction," said the painter. "You can choose whichever you prefer. Both are achievable through my help, certainly not without effort, the difference in this regard is that the feigned acquittal requires a collection of temporary, the abduction requires a much smaller but lasting effort. First, therefore, the feigned acquittal. If you want this, I will write a certification of your innocence on a sheet of paper. The text for such a certification is passed down from my father and is indisputable. With this certification, I then make a round of the judges I know. I start, for example, with the judge I am now painting today, when he comes to the session tonight, I will present the certification to him. I present him with the certification, explain to him your innocence, and swear an oath for your innocence. But this is not merely an external, but a real and binding oath." In the eyes of the painter, it was as if K. had accused him of something. "That would be very kind," said K. "And the judge would believe you and acquit me despite this?" "As I have already said," answered the painter. "By the way, it is not at all certain that everyone would believe me, some judges, for example, will require that I bring you to them. Then you would have to come with me. However, in such a case the matter would already be half won, especially since I would of course instruct you in advance on how to behave with the relevant judge. The situation is worse with those judges who will reject me from the start. On these, we will of course have to give up, even though I will not fail at multiple attempts to win them over, but we can afford to do so, as individual judges cannot sway the outcome." If K. had hoped for the painter to explain anything about the abduction, he was disappointed. The painter said nothing more about this, but continued, "If you prefer the abduction, that is certainly possible. We would have to find a judge who is not too strict and not too generous, otherwise it would be too risky. We would then appear before him in our splendid coach, and when the judge asked where we come from, I would lie and say that we come from a distant country and that we are bringing a rich inheritance to the king, but that we were robbed on the way and lost all our money and valuables. The king, who wants to keep his reputation, would send a messenger to the local constable, the local constable would come to our aid, and we would be allowed to stay in the house of the constable. After a few days, during which we would have to be careful not to give ourselves away, we would offer the constable a large sum of money for his help, in return for which he would protect us and support us in our complaint. Then the constable would have to bring the matter before a judge, who would have to judge us. We would then, with tears in our eyes, tell the judge our story, and I would swear an oath that I am telling the truth. If the judge asked for evidence, I would say that we had already given our money and valuables to the robbers and that we had nothing left to prove our innocence. I would also say that we did not want to accuse anyone and that we had no idea who the robbers were. The judge would then have to decide in our favor, for we would be penniless and hopeless victims, and the king would not want to lose his reputation. And even if the judge asked for evidence, I would say that we had already given our money and valuables to the robbers and that we had nothing left to prove our innocence. I would also say that we did not want to accuse anyone and that we had no idea who the robbers were. However, if the judge did not believe us, he would have to let us go, and we would have to return home, but we would at least have the satisfaction of having caused a scandal, and we would also have the money we brought with us, so that we could return home and start again."

It was a very rainy, stormy morning when K. was in a bad mood about the day ahead and arrived at his office as early as seven o'clock to complete some work before his visit would take it away. He was very tired as he had spent half the night studying Italian grammar to prepare himself a little; the window he had sat at so often recently was more inviting than the desk, but he resisted and sat down to work. Unfortunately, the servant entered and announced that the managing director had sent for him to check if the procurement officer was present; if he was, he was kindly asked to go to the reception room as the Italian was already there. "I am coming," said K., stuffed a small dictionary into his pocket, took an album of city sights he had prepared for the foreigner, and went through the office of the deputy director to the director's office. He was happy to have come to the office so early and to be immediately available, which was probably no one expected. The office of the deputy director was of course still empty, like in the deep night, probably the servant had also been called to the reception room, but it had been unsuccessful. As K. entered the reception room, the two gentlemen rose from the deep armchairs. The director smiled pleasantly, apparently very pleased with K's arrival, he immediately made the introduction, the Italian shook K's hand firmly and smiled, calling someone a morning person. K. didn't understand exactly who he meant, it was also a strange word, whose meaning K only realized later. He answered with a few smooth sentences, which the Italian accepted with a laugh, stroking his grey, bushy moustache nervously several times. This moustache was apparently perfumed, one was almost tempted to get closer and smell it. When everyone was seated and a brief introductory conversation began, K. noticed with great discomfort that he only partially understood the Italian. If he spoke calmly, he understood him almost completely, but those were rare exceptions, usually the speech spilled out of his mouth, he shook his head as if he enjoyed it. In such conversations, however, he always got involved in some dialect that had nothing Italian about it for K, but which the director not only understood but also spoke, which K, however, had probably expected, as the Italian came from southern Italy, where the director had also spent several years. K. realized that the possibility of understanding the Italian was largely taken away from him, as his French was also hard to understand, and the moustache hid the lip movements, which might have helped with understanding. K. began to anticipate many inconveniences, at first he gave it up, wanting to understand the Italian - in the presence of the director, who understood him so easily, it would have been unnecessary effort - and he limited himself to observing him irritably as he relaxed deeply and lightly in the armchair, stroking his short, sharply cut trousers, and once with raised arms and loose jointed hands, trying to show something that K couldn't understand, even though he deliberately didn't look away from his hands. Eventually the Italian looked at the clock and jumped up. After saying goodbye to the director, he pushed himself towards K, so close that K had to push his armchair back to be able to move. The director, who was no doubt aware of the difficulty K was having understanding the Italian, intervened in the conversation and did so cleverly and subtly, giving the impression that he was only adding a few suggestions, while in reality he summarized for K everything that the Italian, who kept talking incessantly, told him, in short. K. learned from him that the Italian had some business to attend to and regrettably would only have little time, that he did not at all intend to rush through all the sights, but had instead decided, if K agreed, to visit only the cathedral in detail. He was very pleased to be able to do so in the company of such a learned and charming man - which was meant to exalt the Italian and quickly grasp the words of the director - and asked him, if the hour was convenient, to meet him in two hours, around ten o'clock, at the cathedral. He himself hoped to be there by then. K. answered appropriately, the Italian shook his hand first with the director, then with K., and then again with the director and left, followed by both, only half paying attention to them and still not stopping talking. K. remained with the director for a while longer, who looked particularly miserable today. He seemed to feel the need to apologize to K and said - they stood close together in private - that he had originally intended to go with the Italian, but then - he gave no further reason - he had decided to send K instead. If he didn't understand the Italian from the start, he shouldn't be surprised, as understanding came very quickly, and if he didn't understand much at all, it wasn't a big deal, as understanding was not that important to the Italian. Besides, K's Italian was surprisingly good, and he would certainly do well with the task. With that, K. was dismissed. The time left to him, he spent by writing down rarely used vocabulary that he needed for the tour of the cathedral. It was a very tedious job, servants brought the mail, officials came with various inquiries and stayed, as they saw K was busy, by the door, but didn't move until they had heard K, the deputy director didn't let it pass him by to disturb K, came in often, took the dictionary from his hand and flipped through it apparently aimlessly, even parties appeared, when the door opened, in the half darkness of the entrance hall and bowed hesitantly - they wanted to draw attention to themselves, but were not sure if they were seen - all this moved around K as if he was the center, while he himself compiled the words he needed, then looked them up in the dictionary, wrote them down, practiced their pronunciation and finally tried to learn them by heart. His once good memory seemed to have deserted him, sometimes he was so angry at the Italian who caused him this effort, that he buried the dictionary under the papers, with the firm intention of not preparing himself anymore, but then he saw that he couldn't be silent with the Italian at the works of art in the cathedral and he pulled the dictionary out again with even greater anger.

The family was entirely engrossed in the violin playing; the landlords, who had initially, hands in their trousers pockets, stood much too close behind the sister's music stand, which surely must have disturbed her, soon withdrew under half-whispered conversations with lowered heads to the window, where they remained, watched over by the father, concerned. It seemed indeed as though they were disappointed in their expectation of hearing a beautiful or entertaining violin performance, had grown tired of the whole spectacle and allowed themselves to be disturbed only out of politeness in their peace. Especially the way they all blew smoke from their cigars skyward suggested great nervousness. And yet the sister played so beautifully. Her face was inclined to the side, scrutinizing and sorrowful, her eyes followed the music notes. Gregor crawled a little further forward and held his head close to the floor, hoping perhaps to meet her eyes. Was he a beast, so affected by the music? It seemed as though the way to the longed-for unknown sustenance was showing itself to him. He was determined to reach the sister, to tug at her dress and thus indicate that she should come to his room with her violin, for no one here rewarded the playing as he wanted to. He didn't want her to leave his room any longer, at least not as long as he lived; his monstrous figure was to be useful to him for the first time; he wanted to be at all the doors of his room at once and to repel the attackers; the sister, however, was not to be forced but to stay voluntarily; she was to sit next to him on the couch, to lean her ear to him, and then he was to confide in her that he had decided to send her to the conservatory, and that he would have told everyone this, if not for the unfortunate incident, on the previous Christmas – Christmas was surely already over? – without worrying about any objections. After this declaration, the sister would burst into tears of emotion, and Gregor would rise up to her shoulder and kiss her neck, which she, since she started her business, wore freely without collar or cravat.

He lost himself on the bench, but his unease continued even in his dreams. Just before sleeping, he remembered that Ippolit would kill ten people, and laughed at the absurdity of the assumption. Around him was a beautiful, clear silence, with one exception - the rustle of leaves, which, it seemed, became even quieter and more secluded in the surrounding area. He dreamt many dreams, and all of them were troubling, causing him to jerk awake. Finally, a woman appeared to him; he knew her, knew her suffering; he could always name her and point to her – but strangely, her face was no longer the same one he always knew, and he did not want to acknowledge her as that woman. In her face was so much remorse and horror, it seemed – she was a dreadful criminal and had just committed a terrible crime. A tear trembled on her pale cheek; she touched him with her hand and pressed her finger to his lips, as if warning him to tread quietly. His heart stopped; he did not want to acknowledge her as a criminal for anything in the world, but he felt that something terrible was about to happen, for the rest of his life. It seemed she wanted to show him something, just beyond, in the park. He stood up to follow her, and suddenly, beneath him, a light, fresh laugh rang out; someone's hand suddenly appeared in his, he grabbed this hand, held it tightly and woke up. Before him stood Aglya, laughing loudly.

The monk said that the traveler couldn't open the gate, so he could only return to the Jade Monastery. The old monk had already been buried, and he was now serving Master Tang in the main hall. Morning services were over, and they were preparing for afternoon services, when suddenly a traveler descended from the sky. The monks bowed and welcomed him into the main hall, where they met Sanzang. Sanzang asked, "Monkey, you've returned. How is your robe?" The traveler replied, "I have a good reason. Earlier, I didn't actually harm these monks. It was that Black Wind Mountain demon who stole it. I went looking for him in secret, only to find him with a white-robed youth and an old man, sitting on a fragrant grassy slope discussing something. He was also a stealthy demon, and he suddenly spoke of a difficult day for his mother in the future, inviting evil spirits to attend his birthday. He obtained a luxurious robe of the Buddha, planning to use it as a shroud and hold a grand feast, called the "Celebration of the Buddha's Robe". I snatched the robe when I arrived, struck him with a staff, and the black demon fled. The old man also disappeared, leaving only the white-robed youth, who was a white flower snake spirit. I hurriedly caught up to him at his cave entrance, challenging him to a duel. He admitted defeat, and I retrieved the robe. The battle lasted half a day, without a clear winner. The demon retreated into his cave, but wanted to eat, and closed the stone door, fearing the battle would continue. I kept looking for Master Tang, first reporting this information, and I now know where Monkey is, so I'm not worried he won't return to me. The monks heard this and clapped their hands together, bowed their heads, and chanted, "Hail to Amitabha Buddha! Today we've found Monkey's whereabouts, and we've been saved!" The traveler said, "You should be cautious in your joy. I haven't yet retrieved Monkey, and Master Tang hasn't yet left his residence. We can only be at ease when Monkey returns and I can send Master Tang out safely. If there's anything you can provide for my master, such as good food and drink, or good grass for the horses, please let me know." The monks all enthusiastically agreed, saying, "We have it! We have it! We have it! Not even a single bit has been neglected!"

As K. passed the corridor separating his office from the main staircase on one of the next evenings – he was going home almost last, only two servants were still working in the dim light of a bulb in the shipping department – he heard sighs emanating from behind a door, behind which he had only ever suspected a storage room, one he had never seen himself – he remained astonished and listened again, to confirm whether he wasn't mistaken – it became quiet for a moment, then the sighs returned.

At first, he wanted to summon one of the servants, perhaps they needed a witness, but then an uncontrollable curiosity seized him, so he actually ripped open the door. It was, as he had correctly assumed, a storage room. Piles of unuseable, old printing press sheets, overturned empty earthen ink bottles lay behind the threshold. In the room itself stood three men, hunched in the low space. A candle fixed to a shelf provided them with light.

"What are you doing here?" K asked, rushed by his agitation, but not loudly. The one man, who seemed to control the others and looked at him first, wore some sort of dark leather clothing that left his neck exposed down to his chest and his entire arms bare. He didn't answer. But the two other men called: "Mr! We are to be beaten because you complained about us to the investigating magistrate." And now K realized, it was indeed Franz and Willem, and the third held a rod to beat them. "Now," said K and stared at them, "I did not complain, I only said how it had happened in my apartment. And without a doubt, you weren't taken away." "Mr," said Willem, while Franz seemed to seek protection behind him from the third, "if you knew how poorly we are paid, you would judge us better. I have a family to feed, and Franz here wanted to marry, one enriches oneself as much as one can, through mere work that's not possible, even with the most strenuous efforts. Your fine laundry tempted me, it's certainly forbidden for guards to act this way, it was wrong, but it's tradition that the laundry belongs to the guards, it's always been that way, don't you think so? It's also understandable, what else would such things mean for one who is unfortunately arrested? If he brings it into the open, then the punishment must be carried out."

"What you're saying now, I didn't know, I did not demand their punishment, I was only concerned with a principle." "Franz," Willem turned to the other guard, "didn't I tell you that the Mr didn't demand our punishment?" Now K heard, and he interrupted himself only to press the rod, which was about to rise again, down, "Stop listening to him," Willem said and interrupted himself only to quickly move his hand, which had received a rod stroke, to his mouth, "we will only be punished because you reported us. Otherwise, nothing would have happened, even if they had found out what we had done. Can that be called justice? We two, especially me, have proven ourselves as guards over a long time – you yourself must admit that we, from the perspective of the authorities, have kept watch well – we had prospects, we would surely have become wardens like this one, who had the good fortune of not being reported by anyone, for such a report comes very seldom. And now, Mr, everything is lost, our careers are over, we will have to perform much lower-ranking tasks than guard duty, and on top of that, we will now receive these dreadful beatings."

"Can the rod cause such pain?" K asked and examined the rod that the warder wielded before him. "We will have to strip completely," Willem said. "Oh really," said K and looked at the warder carefully, he was tanned like a sailor and had a fresh, wild face. "Is there no possibility of sparing the two of them the beatings?" he asked him. "No," said the warder and shook his head laughing. "Undress," he commanded the guards. And to K, he said: "Don't believe everything they say, they are afraid of the beatings and have become somewhat delusional. What this one here, for example, says about his possible career, is almost laughable. Look, how fat he is – the first rod strokes will be lost in the fat. – Do you know, what made him so fat? He has the habit of feeding all the detainees their breakfast. Has he not also eaten your breakfast? I told you that. But a man with such a stomach can never and never become a warder, that's completely out of the question." "There are also warders like that," Willem insisted, who was now in the process of undressing. "No," said the warder and struck him with the rod in such a way that he buckled, "don't listen to him, but undress." "I would reward you well if you let them go," K said and reached for his wallet without looking at the warder again – such transactions are best concluded with lowered eyes – his briefcase. "You want to denounce us too and get us beaten?" said the warder, "no, no!" "Be reasonable," said K, "if I had wanted these two to be punished, I wouldn't want to free them now. I could just slam the door here, not see or hear anything more and go home. Instead, I'm not doing that, on the contrary, I'm sincerely interested in freeing them; if I had known that they were to be punished or even could be punished, I would never have mentioned their names." "So it is!" the guards exclaimed and immediately received a stroke over their already undressed backs. "If you can't prevent their punishment, at least try to free me," Franz said, who maybe in expectation of a favorable outcome of K's intervention had been rather restrained so far, and hung himself low at K's arm and whispered: "My poor bride is waiting for me at the bank, I shame myself terribly." He dried his face, which was flowing with tears, with K's coat. "I waited for no one," the warder said, grabbed the rod with both hands and hit Franz again, while Willem lay huddled in a corner and didn't dare to look up. A scream echoed, which came only from Franz, it didn't sound like a human scream, but like a scream from an instrument that had been tortured, the entire corridor resonated with it, the whole house had to hear it. "Don't scream," K cried, he couldn't hold back, and while he looked in the direction from which the guards had to come, he pushed Franz, not strongly, but strongly enough that the unconscious man fell and rolled on the floor; he avoided the blows, but not entirely, the rod found him on the ground; as he wriggled under it, its tip rose and fell regularly. To prevent the servants from coming, he called: "I am it!" "Good evening, Mr Procurator!" he called back. "Is something wrong?" "No, no," answered K, "it's just a dog barking on the courtyard." As the servants did not move, he added: "You can continue with your work." To avoid having to engage in conversation with the servants, he bent over the window. As he looked again into the corridor after a while, they were already gone. But K remained at the window, he didn't dare to enter the storage room and go home, he wanted to. It was a small rectangular courtyard, into which he looked down, surrounding it were offices, in the distance he saw a servant and a second one appeared shortly after. K closed the window and went home. The next day he handed in his resignation.
