The nature of our hero, however, cannot be said to be so harsh and crude, nor can it be said that his feelings were so dulled that he knew neither pity nor compassion; he felt both, and would have even wished to help, but only if it did not involve a significant sum, if it did not disturb the funds that should not be disturbed; in other words, the fatherly advice: save and keep every penny - it went too far. But he did not cling to the money for the sake of money; he did not hoard and begrudge. No, it was not money that motivated him: he dreamed of a life filled with all pleasures and comforts; carriages, a house, a well-appointed home, delicious meals - this was what constantly filled his mind. He saved every penny in order to eventually taste all of this, in order to eventually enjoy it. The coin was saved sparingly, denied both to himself and others until the time was right. When a rich man passed by him on fast horses and a luxurious harness, he stopped in his tracks and, coming to his senses like after a long sleep, said, "But he was a clerk, he wore his hair in a bun!" And anything that suggested wealth or comfort left an inexplicable impression on him. Having graduated from school, he did not want to take a break: his desire to take on a task and a service was so strong. However, despite the praiseworthy certificates, he had great difficulty finding a place in the civil service. And in remote rural areas, patronage is necessary! He was assigned a small town that brought him thirty or forty rubles a year. But he decided to throw himself wholeheartedly into his service, to win and overcome everything. And indeed, self-denial, patience, and self-restraint showed him an extraordinary example. From early morning to late evening, never tiring of either mental or physical energy, he wrote, drowning in a sea of paperwork, did not go home, slept in the office, sometimes ate with the guards, and yet was able to maintain a sense of dignity, dress properly, give his face a pleasant expression, and even show something noble in his movements. It must be said that civil servants were particularly distinguished by their shabbiness and rudeness. Some had faces like badly baked bread: one cheek was bloated, the other was sunken, the upper lip protruded like a pouch, which, added to everything else, also trembled; in a word, they were far from attractive. They spoke in a harsh, threatening voice, as if they were ready to beat someone; they offered frequent sacrifices to Bacchus, demonstrating in this way that there were still many remnants of paganism in Slavic nature; they sometimes even entered the presence in an intoxicated state, which made the atmosphere in the presence unpleasant and the air far from aromatic. Among such civil servants, Chichikov could not go unnoticed and was distinguished by his cleanliness and politeness, both in his appearance and in his voice, and his total abstinence from any strong drinks. But his path was difficult; he found himself under the command of an elderly and stingy supervisor, who was the embodiment of some cold, unyielding indifference and immovability: he was always the same, an impregnable fortress, never showing a smile in his life, never greeting anyone, not even with a question about health. No one had seen him behave differently, either on the street or at home; he never showed any sign of weakness, never got drunk and laughed in his drunkenness; he never even showed a trace of wild joy, like a robber in his drunken moment, but there was something terrifying in his absence of everything. Nothing was on him equally: neither evil nor good, and something terrible emerged from this absence of everything. Marble-like, featureless face, without any sharp imperfection, did not suggest any resemblance; the features were in perfect proportions to each other. The only constant reminders of his presence were the frequent abscesses and boils, which marked him as one of those people on whom the devil came at night to grind corn. It seemed that there was no human strength to approach such a person and win his favor, but Chichikov tried. At first, he began to accommodate him in all the small matters: carefully examined the quality of his penmanship, prepared several copies in his style, and placed them under his hand each time; swept and straightened his tobacco and sand on the table; provided a new eraser for his inkwell; found his hat, a disgusting hat that had ever existed in the world, and placed it next to him a minute before the end of the session; wiped his back, if he had dirtied it with chalk against the wall, but all of this was done without any notice, as if nothing had happened. Finally, he made inquiries about his domestic life, learned that he had a grown daughter with a similar face, and from this side he devised a plan. He learned that she went to church on Sundays, stood opposite her every time, neatly dressed, with a very messy hairdo - and the plan succeeded: the stern supervisor leaned and called him for tea! And in the office, they had barely turned their heads, when the matter was settled so that Chichikov moved into his house, became a necessary and indispensable person, bought and sugar, treated his daughter like a bride, called the supervisor "father-in-law," kissed his hand; everything in the office praised him, saying that in February before Lent there would be a wedding. The stern supervisor even began to lobby on his behalf with the authorities, and several weeks later Chichikov himself sat as a supervisor in an open position. In this, it seemed, was the main goal of his relations with the old supervisor, because immediately after that, he sent his trunk secretly home and the next day found himself in a new apartment. The supervisor stopped calling him "father-in-law" and no longer kissed his hand, and the wedding matter just faded away, as if nothing had happened. However, whenever he met him, he would squeeze his hand affectionately and invite him for tea, so that the old supervisor, despite his eternal immobility and cold indifference, shook his head every time and whispered to himself, "He blew, he blew, son of the devil!"

Unable, however, to say that the hero's nature was so harsh and crude, or that his feelings had been dulled to such an extent that he knew neither pity nor compassion; he felt both, and would have helped, but only if it did not involve a significant sum, or disturb the funds that should not be disturbed; in other words, the fatherly advice: save and hoard your pennies - it came to naught. Yet, there was no real attachment to the money for the money's sake; he did not control them with a miser's or a hoarder's mentality. Instead, he dreamt of a life of all comforts, with carriages, a house, and delicious meals - these images were constantly in his mind. He saved his pennies with such stubbornness, even denying himself and others, so that he could ultimately savor all of it, in time.

Upon leaving school, he had no intention of taking a break; his desire to start work and serve was so strong. However, despite the praiseworthy recommendations, he struggled to find a place in the government office. In distant provincial towns, connections are essential! The town that came his way was insignificant, with a yearly salary of thirty or forty rubles. Yet, he was determined to take on his work with vigor, to overcome all obstacles. From early morning to late evening, without tiring either mentally or physically, he would write, immersed in reams of paper, not returning home, sleeping in the office, sometimes eating with the guards, and always maintaining his neatness, dressing appropriately, maintaining a pleasant expression on his face, and even displaying a touch of nobility in his movements.

It must be said that the government officials were particularly unsightly and rude. Many had faces as though badly baked bread: their cheeks were bloated on one side, their chins were sunken on the other, their upper lips stuck out like a pouch, and to top it all off, they also trembled. They spoke gruffly, as if they were preparing to punish someone; they frequently offered sacrifices to Bacchus, thus showing that Slavic traditions still held many vestiges of paganism; they often appeared in the presence, not only unkempt but also emitting an unpleasant odor.

Among such officials, Chichikov stood out and was distinguished by his cleanliness and kindness, as well as his total abstention from strong drinks. However, his path was difficult; he came under the supervision of an old, grouchy clerk, who was the embodiment of cold, unyielding indifference and imperturbability: he was always the same, inaccessible, and never once showed a sign of joy, not even on the street or at home; he never once showed any sign of human weakness, not even when drunk and laughing wildly, or giving in to wild revelry, like a robber in his drunken moments. There was something eerie about his absence of any trace of good or evil; something terrifying in his complete lack of everything.

Marble-like coldness and rigidity, without any sharp irregularities, suggested no resemblance; the features of his face were evenly proportioned. In the end, he discovered his home life, learned that he had an adult daughter with a face like his own, and on that score, he hatched a plan. Before the office staff could even turn around, the situation had been resolved so that Chichikov moved into the clerk's home, became an essential and indispensable person, purchased both flour and sugar for him, treated his daughter with the respect due to a bride, and the clerk was referred to as father-in-law, with handshakes and kisses. The grouchy clerk even began to intercede on his behalf with the higher-ups, and after a short time, Chichikov himself became a grouchy clerk, filling a vacant position. The suitcase was sent home secretly, and the next day he found himself in a new apartment. The clerk no longer called him father-in-law and stopped kissing his hand, but the wedding talk died down, as if nothing had happened.

Here Ippolit Kirillovich found it necessary to slightly sketch the character of the deceased Smerdyakov, who "ended his life in a fit of painful delirium and madness." He portrayed him as a feeble-minded man with a hint of some vague formation, confused by philosophical ideas beyond his intellectual capacity and terrified by contemporary teachings about duty and obligation, widely disseminated in practice - the reckless life of his late baron, possibly also his father, Fedor Pavlovich, and theoretically - various strange philosophical conversations with the eldest son of the baron, Ivan Fedorovich, who willingly indulged in this pastime - perhaps out of boredom or the need for mockery, for which he could not find a better outlet. He himself told me about his mental state in the last days of his stay in the house of his baron - explained Ippolit Kirillovich - but witnesses testify to the same effect, including the accused himself, his brother, and even the servant Gregoriy, that is, all those who should have known him very well. In addition, the deceased Smerdyakov was "as frightened as a chicken." "He fell at my feet and kissed my feet - the accused himself told us at the time when he was still not aware of certain disadvantages in such a statement, - it's a chicken in a fit of illness," he expressed himself in his characteristic language. And here is his own accused (who testifies to this) choosing his trusted ones and terrorizing them so much that he finally agrees to serve him as a spy and a courier. In this capacity, the household servant he becomes a traitor, informing the accused of the existence of a packet of money, and of the signs by which one can penetrate to the baron, and in what way he could not help but do so! "They'll kill me, I saw it plainly, that they'll kill me," he said on the stand, shaking and trembling even before us, despite the fact that the one who terrorized him was already under arrest at the time and could no longer punish him. "I was suspected every minute - he himself said in fear and trembling, eager only to appease their anger, to inform them of any secret - to be able to see my innocence before them and be released alive for repentance." Here are his own words, which I wrote down and remember: "When they would shout at me, I would fall on my knees before them and faint." Highly honest by nature, this young man entered the trust of his baron, who distinguished his honesty when he returned his lost money, unfortunate Smerdyakov, one must assume, suffered greatly from remorse for his betrayal of his baron, whom he loved like his benefactor. Those who suffer from epilepsy, according to the testimony of the deepest psychiatrists, are always prone to persistent and, of course, painful self-blame. They torment themselves over their "guilt" in something and before someone, torment themselves with pangs of conscience, often, even without any basis, exaggerate and even invent various guilt and crimes for themselves. And here is such a subject becomes truly guilty and criminal out of fear and intimidation. In addition, he had a strong premonition that something evil was coming out of the circumstances that were unfolding before his eyes. When the eldest son of Fedor Pavlovich, Ivan Fedorovich, was about to leave for Moscow just before the disaster, Smerdyakov begged him to stay, but, however, could not, out of cowardice, express all his fears in clear and categorical terms. He was content with hints, but the hints were not understood. It should be noted that in Ivan Fedorovich he saw some kind of protection, some kind of guarantee, that as long as he was there, nothing bad would happen. Remember the expression in "drunk" letter Dmitri Karamazov: "I'll kill the old man, if only Ivan goes away"; apparently, the presence of Ivan Fedorovich seemed to everyone like some kind of guarantee of peace and order in the house. And here he goes away, and Smerdyakov falls immediately, almost an hour after the young baron leaves, into a fit of illness. But this is perfectly understandable. Here it is necessary to mention that, disheartened by fears and some kind of despair, Smerdyakov in the last days felt the possibility of the approach of fits of illness, which had always happened to him in moments of moral tension and shock. The day and hour of these fits could not be guessed, but every epileptic can feel the predisposition to a fit in advance. Such is the word of medicine. And just as he was leaving the yard, Ivan Fedorovich, Smerdyakov, under the impression of his, so to speak, orphanhood and his vulnerability, went to the household chores in the basement, went down the stairs and thought: "Will there be a fit or not? And what if it comes now?" And it is precisely from this state of mind, from this self-torment, from these questions and seizures that the neck spasm, always preceding a fit, seizes him, and he flies headlong unconscious to the bottom of the cellar. And here, in this natural case, they try to see some kind of suspicion, some kind of hint, some kind of indication, that he feigned illness deliberately! But if deliberately, then the question arises: for what purpose? What calculation, with what aim? I am already not talking about medicine; science, allegedly, lies, science makes mistakes - doctors could not distinguish truth from pretense, but answer me, gentlemen jurors, the question: for what purpose did he pretend to be ill? Not to kill, you see, surely not for that. But what if he pretended to be ill to attract immediate and quick attention in the house? See, gentlemen jurors, in the house of Fedor Pavlovich on the night of the crime there were and were staying five people: first, Fedor Pavlovich himself, but of course he did not kill himself, that's clear; second, his servant Gregoriy, but almost killed him; third, his wife Gregori's, the servant Marfa Ignatievna, but it's shameful to suggest that she could be a murderer. The rest, it seems, are two people: the accused and Smerdyakov. But since the accused swears that he did not kill, then, it seems, Smerdyakov had to kill, there is no other way, and because there is no one else to find, another murderer. Hence, it is precisely from this "cunning" and colossal accusation that this unfortunate, who recently took his own life, idiot fell! Even if there was a shadow, a hint, a suspicion of some other person, someone else, I am convinced that even the accused would have pointed to Smerdyakov then, for he would have been ashamed to accuse him of this murder. Translation Note:
This passage describes a fight between the Tang Seng (Qi Tian Da Sheng) and a Taoist monk (Li Cha, a.k.a Cross-wielding) who tries to capture him. The Taoist monk comes from the Li family, which is one of the Three Pure Ones (Sandie Jing) of Taoism. The fight is taking place outside the Buddhist palace gate.

Cross-wielding's name suggests that he uses two weapons (he may also be known as "Sword-wielding Li" and "Axe-wielding Li"). The ruyi staff used by Qi Tian Da Sheng is an important symbol in Chinese Buddhism, representing wisdom, authority, and good fortune.

The phrase "do faquan," (辄敢问) means "dare to ask" or "have the audacity to ask," and is used to convey the notion of someone questioning someone in a position of authority, in a way that is not appropriate. The term "military affairs" (junqi) here refers to the situation in the Tang Dynasty, where the Buddhist monks were competing against the Taoist monks and the Daoist priests for followers.

I was so taken aback by his proposal that I myself do not know why I cried. He took my tears as gratitude and said that he had always been certain that I was kind, sensitive, and learned young woman, but that he had only recently resolved to take such a step after learning in detail about my current behavior. Here he asked about you, said that he had heard everything, that you were a noble person, that he himself did not want to be in debt to you and that five hundred rubles for everything I had done for him would be enough? When I explained to him what I had done for me, which no amount of money could pay, he said that it was all nonsense, that it was all romance, that I was still young and read poetry, that romances ruin young girls, that books only corrupt morality, and that he could not stand any books; he advised me to live through his years and then talk about people; "then, he added, you will learn about people". Then he said that I should think carefully about his proposals, that it would be very unpleasant for him if I made such an important step impulsively, that impulsiveness and infatuation ruin the inexperienced youth, but that he extremely wanted a favorable response from my side, that, finally, in case of refusal, he would be forced to marry a merchant woman in Moscow because, he said, I had sworn to disinherit a good-for-nothing nephew. He left me without warning, leaving five hundred rubles, as he said, for expenses; said that I would get fat in the village like a pancake, that I would slide around him like cheese in butter, that he now had a lot of trouble, that he had been working all day on business and that he had now taken a break to come to me. Here he left. I thought for a long time, I thought many times, I suffered, thinking, friend, finally I decided. Friend, I will marry him, I must agree to his proposal. If anyone can save me from my shame, restore my honorable name, protect me from poverty, hardship, and misfortune in the future, then it is only him. What am I to expect from the future, what else to ask of fate? Fedora says that I should not lose my happiness; says – what is happiness if not this? At least I do not see another way for myself, my priceless friend. What should I do? I have ruined my health with work; I cannot work constantly. Going to people? – I am about to wither with grief, and besides, I am not attractive to anyone. I am sick by nature, and therefore I will always be a burden on others' hands. Of course, I am not going to heaven now, but what should I do, friend, what should I do? What am I to choose from?

He took my tears for gratitude and told me that he had always been certain that I was a good, sensitive, and learned young woman, but that he had not resolved to take such a step until he learned in full detail about my current behavior. Here he asked about you, said he had heard everything, that you were a noble person, that he, on his part, did not want to be in your debt and that 500 rubles would be enough for everything you had done for him? When I explained to him what you had done for me, that no amount of money could compensate for it, he said it was all nonsense, that it was all novels, that I was still young and reading poetry, that novels ruin young girls, that books only corrupt morality and that he could not endure any books; he advised me to live through his years and then to speak of people; "then," he added, "you will know people." Then he said that I should think carefully about his proposals, that it would be very unpleasant for him if I made such an important step impulsively, added that impulsiveness and infatuation ruin an inexperienced youth, but that he was extremely eager for a favorable response from my side, that, finally, if it was not the case, he would be forced to marry a merchant's daughter in Moscow, because, he says, I swore to deprive the worthless nephew of his inheritance. He left me forcibly with 500 rubles, as he said, for clothes; said that I would get fat in the village like a loaf of bread, that I would slide like cheese in butter with him, that he now had a lot of trouble, that he had spent a whole day on business and that he had now slipped in between for me. Then he left. I thought for a long time, I reconsidered a lot, I suffered, thinking, friend, at last I decided. Friend, I will marry him, I must agree to his proposal. If someone can free me from my shame, restore my honorable name, protect me from poverty, hardship and misfortune in the future, then only he can. What am I to expect from the future, what else to ask of fate? Fedora says that losing happiness is not necessary; she says, what is happiness called in such a case? At least I do not find another way for myself, my precious friend. What am I to do? I have ruined my health with work; I cannot work constantly. To go to people? - I wither from longing, besides, I am not pleasing to anyone. I am sick by nature, and therefore I will always be a burden on other people's hands. Of course, I am not going to heaven now, but what am I to do, friend, what am I to do? From what to choose for me?

Nevertheless, there were moments of content and semi-consciousness. On which paths! he then thought with alarm. On which paths! Just as any man, whose natural merits kindled an aristocratic interest in his lineage, he was accustomed to reflecting on the achievements and successes of his life in terms of his ancestors, seeking their approval, their satisfaction, their reluctant respect in spirit. He thought of them now too, entangled in such an unseemly experience, ensnared in such exotic excesses of emotion; thought of their stern rectitude, their noble masculinity, and sighed heavily. What would they say? But of course, what could they have said about his entire life, which had strayed so far from them, to this life enslaved to art, about which he himself once, in the sense of the fathers, had made such scathing adolescent judgments, and which was essentially similar to theirs! He too had served, he too had trained himself rigorously; he too was a soldier and a warrior, just like many of them—for art was a war, a grueling struggle, for which one no longer lasted long today. A life of self-overcoming and defiance, a harsh, steadfast, and abstinent life, which he had fashioned as a symbol for a delicate and contemporary heroism—well, he could call it manly, could call it brave, and it seemed as if the Eros that mastered him was somehow particularly compatible and inclined to such a life. Had he not stood in high esteem among the bravest of peoples, yes, was it not said that he had bloomed in their cities through bravery? Numerous heroes of the past had willingly borne his yoke, for no humiliation was greater than the one imposed by God, and deeds that would have been considered marks of cowardice if they had been done for other purposes—limping, swearing, insistent pleas, and servile nature—these did not bring shame upon the lover, but rather earned him praise instead.

The Bodhisattva led the crowd into the room, paid respects to the Jade Emperor, also greeted the Old Immortal and Queen Mother, and they all sat down. The Bodhisattva asked, "How did the Peach Banquet go?" The Jade Emperor replied, "It is held annually, full of joy and happiness. However, this year, the monkey king caused chaos, making it an empty gathering." The Bodhisattva asked, "Where does the monkey king come from?" The Jade Emperor replied, "The monkey king is from the Country of the Flower-Fruit Mountain on the East Victory Gods Continent, who was born from a stone egg. At birth, he emitted a golden radiance, clashing against the heavenly mansion. Initially, he did not care, but later, he cultivated himself, subdued dragons and tigers, and eliminated his spiritual bonds. At that time, the Dragon King and the King Yama announced him. I wanted to capture him, but the Longgan star announced, 'In the three realms, those with nine openings can become immortal.' I then taught him and proclaimed his elevation, appointing him as the Inspector of the Imperial Stables, the Commissioner of the Imperial Horse Guards. He resented the low-ranking position and rebelled against heaven. I then dispatched Li the Heavenly King and the Son of the Yellow Emperor to subdue him, and issued an edict to restore order, proclaiming his appointment as 'The Great Sage, Equal to Heaven', but with no actual power. He had nothing to do, so he roamed east and west. I was afraid of further incidents, so I entrusted him to manage the Peach Garden. He did not obey the laws, plundered the old trees and big peaches. When the banquet was set, he was not present, and he tricked the Red-shod Immortal to attend, changing his appearance to infiltrate the banquet, stealing all the immortal food and drinks, stealing the Queen Mother's elixir, and stealing several bottles of imperial wine, to enjoy with the monkeys on the local mountain." The Jade Emperor lamented, "I am troubled by this matter, thus I summoned ten million celestial troops, setting up a net over the earth and sky to capture him. I have not heard any news today, and I am not sure of the outcome."

The Bodhisattva led the crowd inside, paid respects to the Jade Emperor, and then greeted the Old Man and the Queen Mother, each taking their seats. The Bodhisattva asked, "How was the peach banquet?" The Jade Emperor replied, "It is held annually, filled with joy and laughter. However, this year, it was disrupted by the monkey king, making it a mockery indeed." The Bodhisattva asked, "Where did the monkey king come from?" The Jade Emperor replied, "The monkey king is a monkey who was born on the Flower-Fruit Mountain in the Cloud-Egg Country of the Eastern Victory Gods. Upon his birth, he emitted golden light and fought his way through the Heavenly Office. At first, he did not care, but soon he became skillful, subduing dragons and tigers, and even killed his own lineage. When the dragon kings and the kings of hell performed, I attempted to capture him. The Longgan Star gave a sign, saying, 'In the three realms, those with nine apertures can become immortal.' I then taught him, promoted him to the post of Royal Steward, and appointed him the Inspector of the Royal Horses. However, he disliked the petty official work, rebelled against the heavenly palace. I then appointed Li the Heavenly King and the Son of the Dragon King to subdue him, and I issued an edict to pacify the region, promoting him to the title of 'Heavenly Monkey King,' but he only received an official rank but no income. Because he had nothing to do, he roamed east and west. I was worried about other incidents, so I entrusted him with the management of the Peach Garden. He disregarded the laws, stealing and eating the ripe peaches from the ancient trees. By the time of the banquet, he was no longer an official, not even invited. He schemed to lure the Red-Footed Immortal, disguising himself as an immortal, and stole all the immortal food and wine, even stealing the Queen Mother's immortality elixir and the palace wine, and enjoyed them with the monkeys on the mountain. I am troubled by this and have dispatched ten thousand heavenly troops, setting up a net over heaven and earth to capture him. I have not heard any news of the outcome today."

Bodhisattva leads the crowd inside, bows to Jade Emperor, and also greets Lao Jun and Queen Mother, each taking a seat. They ask, "How was the Peach Banquet?" Bodhisattva asked, "Where does the monkey king come from?" Bodhisattva leads the crowd into the interior, bows to Jade Emperor and greets the Old Man of the Mountain and Queen Mother, who take their seats. Jade Emperor replies, "The monkey king was born from a stone egg on the Flower-Fragrant Peak in the Eastern Paradise of the Immortals. However, he only received the title but no actual power. Bored, he wandered east and west. I was worried about further mischief, so I entrusted him with the management of the Peach Blossom Spring. He, however, did not abide by the law, stealing and eating the ripe peaches from the ancient trees. By the time of the gathering, he was a commoner and had not been invited. I am troubled by this and have sent ten thousand heavenly soldiers to apprehend him. I have not heard any report today, and I do not know the outcome."

I have not received a report from them yet, and do not know the outcome."

A cacophony of copper snake and iron dog, vying for dominion at the dinner table, forever consigned to fall into the depths of the Nai River, with no escape. The verse goes: At times, one hears the cries of ghosts and the signals of gods, blood and water surging high in waves. Hordes of headless cattle and horses, grotesque and menacing, stand guard at the Nai River Bridge. Just as the discussion was underway, those bridge attendants had already left. The emperor's heart trembled with fear, nodding silently in resignation, mournfully brooding, accompanied by the judge and the grand councilor, crossing the malevolent waters of the Nai River, entering the "Cemetery of Unjust Death." Once more, they arrived at the city of False Execution, hearing the uproar of people, clearly saying "Li Wemin has arrived! Li Wemin has arrived!" The emperor listened to the calls, his heart pounding with fear. Upon seeing a group of ghosts with twisted limbs and headless bodies, he moved forward to confront them, all of them crying out: "Return my life to me! Return my life to me!" In a panic, the emperor hid himself, only calling out "Cui Xianghua save me! Cui Xianghua save me!" The judge said: Your Majesty, these people are all from the sixty-four locations of smoke and dust, the seventy-two locations of grass bandits, the ghosts of the princes and the heads of the clans. They are all victims of false accusations, without justice or mercy, unable to be reincarnated, and with no money or silver to bribe, all are lonely, hungry ghosts. Your Majesty, if you give them some money and silver, I can save them. The emperor said: "My humble self has come here with an empty body, where am I to find money and silver?" The judge said: "Your Majesty, there is someone in the daytime, with gold and silver in abundance, who has deposited it in my presence. Your Majesty could establish a contract, the small judge could act as a guarantor, and borrow from him a storehouse, to disperse these hungry ghosts, and you will be able to pass through. The judge then instructed: "This gold and silver, you can all divide and use as needed, to guide your Great Tang Emperor across, his vital energy is still strong. I have received ten thousand words from the Immortal, to send his spirit back, to teach him to establish a water and land gathering in the Yellower Heaven, to guide you to reincarnation, and to rest in peace again." The ghosts, upon hearing this, took the gold and silver and retreated. The judge ordered the grand councilor to shake the banner of the spirits, and led the emperor out of the city of False Execution, racing up the Plain of Yang, disappearing into the distance. In the end, it is unknown from what road they came, to be continued.

The Bronze Snake and Iron Dog vie for food, doomed to forever fall into the treacherous river Nai. The poem reads: Sometimes the wailing of ghosts can be heard together with the sound of gods, blood and water filling the waves high. Countless cow heads and horses faces stand fierce as guards of the Nai River bridge. Just as the conversation was ongoing, those few bridge attendants had already left. The Emperor's heart trembled again, nodding in solemn agreement, deeply sorrowful, following the judge and the Grand Councilor, crossing the treacherous waters of the Nai River and reaching the Blood Basin of Suffering. Again, they arrived at the city of False Execution, only to hear cries and shouts of people. Clearly they were saying, "Li Wenmin has arrived! Li Wenmin has arrived!" The Emperor heard the call, his heart pounding with fear. Upon seeing a group of beings with slouched backs and twisted limbs, headless ghosts, advancing to block the way, they all pleaded, "Return my life! Return my life!" The Emperor, panicking, only called out, "Save me, Qiu Sir! Save me, Qiu Sir!" The judge said, "Your Majesty, those beings are from the sixty-four places of smoke and dust, seventy-two places of grass bandits, the ghosts of all the princes and heads. They are all unjust deaths, with no accountability, no chance of reincarnation, and no wealth to use as payment, all are lonely, hungry ghosts. Your Majesty must offer them some wealth to use, and I can save them. Your Majesty is short of money, but in my underworld there is a man with gold and silver, storing it for safekeeping. Your Majesty can make a decree to take some of his gold and silver, borrow it for a while, to feed these hungry ghosts and pass by. Your Majesty wonders who this man is?" The judge said, "He is a man from the Henan Kaifeng government, surnamed Xiang and named Liang, he has thirteen storage houses of gold and silver here. If Your Majesty borrows from him, just return it when you leave the underworld." The Emperor was overjoyed, willing to make a decree to borrow from him. Thus, a decree was made with the judge, borrowing his gold and silver, and entrusting the Grand Councilor to distribute it. The judge then ordered, "This gold and silver, you all can divide and use wisely, bring Your Majesty across the Nai River, his life is still long. I have received ten jin of silver tongue language, to send his spirit back, to teach him to create a water and land great meeting in the afterlife, to help you cross over and reincarnate again." The ghosts heard the words, received the gold and silver, and all retreated uniquely. The judge ordered the Grand Councilor to shake the soul flag, leading the Emperor out of the False Execution city, running up the Plain Yang Road, drifting away. Ultimately, it is not known where he came from on that road, to be continued next time.

Hear cries of ghosts and the roar of gods, a sea of blood and waves high as ten thousand steps. Countless heads of cattle and horses stand fierce, guarding the bridge of the Na River. Just as one was speaking, the messengers from the bridge vanished. The emperor's heart trembled with anxiety, nodded, murmured a sigh, sorrowfully following the judge and the grand guardian, crossing the evil water of the Na River, entering the Cauldron of Blood. Later, they arrived at the city of Wrongful Death, only to hear shouts of people, clearly saying "Li Zhimin is here! Li Zhimin is here!" The emperor heard the calls, his heart pounded with fear. Seeing a group of figures with limbs twisted and broken, headless spirits, they stepped forward to stop them, all called out: "Give me back my life! Give me back my life!"

Terrified, the emperor hid and only cried out: "Qiu Sir, save me! Qiu Sir, save me!" The judge said: "Your Majesty, those people are the spirits of the Sixty-four Dusty Realms and Seventy-two Grassy Bandits, the ghosts of all the princes and chieftains. They are all guilty of Wrongful Death, with no salvation or punishment, unable to reincarnate, and also without money or currency, all are lonely and hungry ghosts. Your Majesty should give them some money and currency, and I can save them. Your Majesty asked: "But where am I supposed to find money and currency?" The judge said: "Your Majesty, there is a person in the daylight with gold and silver, in my dark hall they are kept. Your Majesty can establish a convention, the minor judge can serve as a guarantor, and borrow a basket of it to scatter these hungry ghosts, allowing you to pass. Your Majesty asked: "Who is this person?" The judge said: "He is a man from the Kaifeng Prefecture, surnamed Xiao, with the name Liang. He has thirteen baskets of gold and silver here. If Your Majesty borrows and returns it later in the daylight, everything will be fine." The emperor was overjoyed and wished to borrow it. He thus made a decree with the judge, borrowing a basket of gold and silver, and with the grand guardian, they scattered it. The judge then ordered: "This gold and silver should be divided and used carefully, for the use of the Tang Emperor, he is still young. I have received ten pounds of gold and silver, to send him back to the daylight, teach him to hold a water-land assembly, to help you reincarnate, and to rest again." The spirits heard the words, received the gold and silver, and retreated one by one. The judge ordered the grand guardian to wave the spirit flag, leading the emperor out of the city of Wrongful Death, rushing up the Plain of Yang, and departing. In the end, it is not known where they came from, and we will continue next time.

Hearing the cries of spirits and the responses of the gods, the waves of blood-colored water towered high, countless ox heads and horse faces stood menacingly guarding the Nai River Bridge. Just as the conversation was ongoing, the bridge messengers had already returned. Emperor Taizong's heart trembled in fear, bowed his head in dismay, and mournfully followed the judge and the deputy. They had crossed the evil waters of the Nai River, passing into the Kuei Kingdom. Once more, they arrived at the City of Unjust Death, and all one could hear were cries and shouting, clearly saying "Li Wenmin has come! Li Wenmin has come!" Hearing the call, Emperor Taizong's heart was filled with terror. As a crowd of disembodied spirits with heads and limbs missing approached, he rushed forward to confront them, crying "Give me back my life! Give me back my life!" Taizong hid in fear, only calling out "Save me, Qiu Sir! Save me, Qiu Sir!" The judge said: "Your Majesty, these people are the spirits of the sixty-four places of smoke and dust, the seventy-two places of grass bandits, the ghosts of the crown princes, the ghosts of the heads of state; they are all victims of unjust deaths, with no retribution or justice, unable to reincarnate, and no money or copper coins to bind them, they are all lonely and hungry ghosts. Your Majesty needs some money and copper coins to buy them off. Only then can I save you." Taizong said: "Empty-handed, how can I have money and copper coins here?" The judge said: "Your Majesty, there is a man in the world of the living, with gold and silver, who has left it in my jurisdiction. Your Majesty can make a proclamation and set up a convention, and the small judge can serve as a guard, and borrow some of it to scatter these hungry ghosts, thus enabling us to pass on.

Who is this man?" The judge said: "He is a man from the city of Kaifeng in Henan, named Xiao and surnamed Liu, he has thirteen stores of gold and silver here. If Your Majesty borrows some of it and returns it when you are in the world of the living, it will be fine." Taizong was very pleased and was eager to make a proclamation to borrow it. The document was drafted, and Taizong borrowed the gold and silver from Xiao and Liu, entrusting the deputy to distribute it. The judge then ordered: "This gold and silver, you can all divide and use wisely, lead your great Tang Emperor across, his life still remains early. I have received ten thousand pieces of speech from him, to send him back to the world of the living, to make him a water and land assembly, to enable us to reincarnate, and to rest in peace." — That's exactly how it was, — grimly confirmed Rogozhin, — Zalozev also told me that back then. I was crossing the Neva on the third day of my father's funeral, and she stepped out from a shop, got into a carriage. That's how I was scorched. I ran into Zalozev, who didn't acknowledge me, walked like a shop clerk from a barber, and winked at me, while we stood out among our parents in greasy boots and felt hats. He told me that she wasn't my wife, he called her Princess Nastasya Filipovna, her surname was Barashkova, and she lived with Toksky, and Toksky can't get rid of her now, as she has reached the age of true maturity, fifty-five, and wants to marry the most beautiful woman in all of St. Petersburg. It was then that he suggested that I could see Nastasya Filipovna at the Bolshoi Theater today, in the ballet, in her box, in the foyer, she would be sitting. Try to go to the ballet with our parents, he said, it'll be a disaster! I, however, sneaked away silently for an hour and saw Nastasya Filipovna again; I didn't sleep all night. The next day the deceased gave me two five-percent bonds, each worth five thousand, to sell and pay off seven thousand five hundred to the Andreevs at their office, keep the remaining change without going anywhere, and bring it to me. I sold the bonds, took the money, but didn't go to the Andreevs' office, instead, I went, looking nowhere, to an English store and picked out four hundred rubles' worth of trinkets, one diamond in each, so they'd be almost like nuts. Four hundred rubles were left, I gave my name, they believed me. With the trinkets, I went to Zalozev: here you go, brother, let's go to Nastasya Filipovna. We left. I don't know what was under my feet, what was in front of me, what was on the sides - I don't know and don't remember. We walked straight to her in the hall, she came to us. I didn't dare to say that it was I, the one and only; "From Porfiry, by the way, Rogozhin," said Zalozev, "remember our meeting yesterday; please accept my greetings." She opened it, looked, smiled: "Thank you for your kind attention to your friend, Mr. Rogozhin," she said, and turned away and left. Why didn't I die then and there! If I had gone, it was because I thought: "I'll be dead anyway!" What was most painful to me was that this beast Zalozev took it all upon himself. I was short, dressed like a clown, stood there, silent, looking at her with shameful eyes, while he was well-dressed, with pomade and curled hair, rosy-cheeked, wearing a checkered cravat, and he spread out, he opened up, and I'm sure she took him instead of me! "Well," I said, "you'll have to explain this to Semen Porfiryevich later!" She laughed: "And how are you going to explain this to Semen Porfiryevich?" I wanted to throw myself into the water, not going home, but thought: "I'll be dead anyway", and turned home like a madman.
